items.title: Tapyr documentation
items.text:
Tapyr is an open source, self-hosted gateway that turns the REST APIs of cloud-managed network gear into Prometheus and OTLP metrics. One declarative definition per API, in YAML and CEL, and every call planned against the vendor's rate limits and quotas.

New to Tapyr? The project site, tapyr.eu, shows what it does and why in a few minutes.

InstallBinaries, container image and deployment. Getting startedCollect metrics from a simulated API in ten minutes, with the binary alone. ProvidersOne package per vendor API: what it collects, its limits and its dashboard. GitHubSource, releases and issues.

items.title: Alerts
items.text:
Tapyr exposes its own metrics on /metrics/self (see 07-self-observability.md). The example rules in examples/alerts/tapyr-alerts.yaml turn them into alerts for Prometheus or vmalert. They are starting points: copy them, then tune the thresholds and durations to your job intervals and quotas.

# prometheus.yml
rule_files:
  - /etc/prometheus/rules/tapyr-alerts.yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: tapyr
    metrics_path: /metrics/self
    honor_labels: true   # the self-metrics carry the job label of the Tapyr job
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["tapyr:9790"]

honor_labels: true matters: without it, the scrape renames the job label of the self-metrics (the name of the Tapyr job) to exported_job, and the alerts lose it. TapyrDown expects the scrape job to be named tapyr.

The rules are checked and unit tested with promtool (make alerts-check, in CI). A Go test checks that every metric they use is a documented self-metric and that every alert has its section below.

Severities: critical needs someone now (collection stopped or about to), warning needs someone today, info is worth a look.

items.title: TapyrDown
items.text: Nothing answered the scrape of /metrics/self for 5 minutes: the process is down, restarting in a loop, or unreachable. Check the logs of the container or service (tapyr run logs as JSON on stderr) and GET /healthz.

items.title: TapyrReauthRequired
items.text: The credentials of an account can no longer be renewed (for example an Aruba Central refresh token that expired or was revoked), so its jobs stopped. Generate new credentials for the account (for Aruba, a new token pair under API Gateway > System Apps & Tokens, or My Apps & Tokens), update the secret, and reload the configuration (SIGHUP, or docker kill -s HUP <container>). The overview of the UI and GET /api/v1/accounts show the account concerned.

items.title: TapyrJobStale
items.text: A job has not succeeded for three of its effective intervals. Open the job in the UI (Jobs) or GET /api/v1/jobs/{name}/runs for the errors of its last runs: authentication (401, 403), a changed API (mapping errors), a provider outage (open circuit), or a quota that pauses it (see the quota alerts).

items.title: TapyrJobLagging
items.text: The runs of a job start more than one interval after their schedule: requests wait for rate or concurrency limits, or the job takes longer than its interval. tapyr_budget_wait_seconds and the Provider calls row of the tapyr-overview dashboard show where the time goes. Raise the interval of the job or of the jobs that share the limit.

items.title: TapyrCircuitOpen
items.text: Repeated failures opened the circuit of an account or a target: Tapyr stopped calling it and probes again on its own after the cooldown. The alert lasts while the provider (or the device, for RutOS) keeps failing. Check that the endpoint is reachable from Tapyr and that the provider status page shows no incident.

items.title: TapyrQuotaAlmostExhausted
items.text: Less than 5% of a quota is left before its reset. The planner already pauses the low-priority jobs; critical jobs stop when the quota is spent. If Tapyr is the only client, the plan was too optimistic: check tapyr plan. Otherwise another client consumes the same quota (tapyr_budget_external_usage).

items.title: TapyrQuotaExhaustionProjected
items.text: At the current pace, a quota runs out within 6 hours, before its reset. The usual cause is another client using the same credentials or organization: its consumption shows as external usage in the Budgets page of the UI. Lower the priority or raise the interval of jobs, or give Tapyr its own credentials.

items.title: TapyrPlanInfeasible
items.text: The critical jobs do not fit a quota at their desired interval, even with every other job paused. tapyr plan (or the Plan page) lists the jobs and their consumption: raise intervals, reduce the fan-out (forEach.maxInstances, filters), or ask the provider for a larger quota.

items.title: TapyrUnexpected429
items.text: A provider returned 429 Too Many Requests that no declared limit predicted. Either the provider definition misses a limit (or declares it too high), or another client shares the credentials. Tapyr honors Retry-After and backs off, but the definition should be fixed: open an issue with the provider, the endpoint and the headers of the response (the debug endpoint shows them, secrets redacted).

items.title: TapyrLimitMismatch
items.text: The quota headers of a provider announce a maximum different from the one declared in its definition. Tapyr follows the headers; update the limit in the provider definition (max: auto with initialMax when the maximum depends on the account) so that tapyr plan is accurate.

items.title: TapyrOutputDropping
items.text: A push output (remote write or OTLP) drops samples: queue_full when the backend is slower than the collection, rejected or out_of_order when it refuses them. tapyr_output_send_failures_total gives the class of the errors; for out_of_order, check that no other writer sends the same series.

items.title: TapyrOutputFailing
items.text: A push output has not delivered anything for 10 minutes, or keeps failing without having ever delivered (a wrong URL or credentials from the start). The samples wait in the bounded queue, and the oldest are dropped when it is full. Check that the backend is up and reachable, and its authentication.

items.title: TapyrConfigReloadFailed
items.text: The last reload of the configuration was rejected; the previous configuration keeps running. tapyr validate --config <paths> prints every error with its file and line.

items.title: TapyrStateFlushFailing
items.text: Tapyr cannot write its state store (SQLite): quota consumption, rotated tokens and counters since the last flush would be lost on restart, and rotated Aruba tokens could be lost for good. Check the free space and the permissions of the state path (settings.state.path).

items.title: Concepts
items.text: Tapyr polls the APIs of vendor platforms and turns their answers into metrics. What makes it different from a script with a loop is that it treats the API quota as a budget: the limits of every API are declared once, every request is accounted against them, and the polling slows down on purpose before a quota runs out. This page explains the pieces and how they fit; the specification has the full detail.

items.title: Configuration documents
items.text:
A configuration is a set of YAML documents, in one file or many, in a directory or several. Every document has the same envelope:

apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
kind: Account          # the kind of the document
metadata:
  name: campus         # unique per kind
spec: {}               # depends on the kind
Kind Written by What it is Provider provider packages An API: its base URL, authentication, pagination, error semantics and rate limits JobTemplate provider packages A reusable request and its mapping to metrics Account you An instance of a provider, with its credentials, parameters, targets and labels Job you What to collect for an account, from a template (or inline), at which interval and priority Output you Where the samples go: Prometheus scrape, remote write or OTLP Settings you, optionally Server, state store, retries, logs and other global settings

You write the last four. tapyr validate checks every document against its JSON Schema and reports every error with its file, line and column. The configuration reference lists every field.

items.title: Provider packages
items.text:
A provider package describes one vendor API: the Provider document, its JobTemplates, a simulator with fault scenarios, a contract test, a Grafana dashboard and a README. Packages are YAML and CEL, never Go code (authentication flows that cannot be declared are the exception, as Go auth plugins). The built-in packages are compiled into the binary; tapyr provider list shows them, and settings.providerPaths adds packages of your own.

The same definition drives the collector and the simulator: tapyr sim serves an API that behaves like the real one, with its authentication, pagination and limits, so you can try a configuration and its quota consumption without an account.

items.title: Accounts and targets
items.text:
An Account instantiates a provider with what that provider asks for: params (an organization, a base URL) and secrets. Secrets are never written in the configuration: they are references to environment variables or files.

spec:
  provider: meraki-dashboard
  secrets:
    apiKey: { env: TAPYR_MERAKI_API_KEY }    # or { file: /run/secrets/meraki }
  labels:
    tenant: campus                           # added to every sample of the account

Some APIs live on each device rather than in a cloud, like the local API of Teltonika routers. A multi-target account lists the devices as targets; every job of the account then runs once per target, and each target can override the params, secrets and labels of the account.

When other tools share the same credentials, budget.share limits Tapyr to a part of every quota (share: 0.5 leaves half for the others).

items.title: Jobs
items.text:
A Job collects one thing for one account, usually by naming a template of the provider package:

spec:
  account: campus
  template: meraki-device-availabilities
  interval: 5m           # the desired interval, defaults to the template's
  priority: high         # critical, high, normal (default) or low

The interval is a wish: the planner may stretch it to fit the quotas (see below). The priority decides who slows down first. A job sends its samples to every output, or to the subset in outputs; labels are added to its samples, and win over target and account labels.

items.title: Discovery
items.text:
Many APIs are hierarchical: organizations contain networks, networks contain devices, and the URL of a request needs the identifier of its parent. An inventory template (role: inventory, or both when it also produces metrics) lists items; a template with forEach runs once per item of its parent, with the variables of the item in its request:

organizations (inventory) -> networks (inventory, one instance per organization) -> devices (one instance per network)

These per-item runs are instances of the job. You only declare the job you want: parents that no job of the account instantiates run implicitly, named <account>.<template>, at priority low. The inventory is cached in the state store, so a restart does not wait for discovery; the instances of a fan-out are spread over their interval instead of firing together (a newly discovered one runs first within the jitter, then at its point of the interval), and forEach.maxInstances (default 10000) protects against a runaway discovery.

items.title: Mapping
items.text:
A template maps the JSON of a response to samples with CEL expressions: which list holds the items, and for every metric its value and labels.

extract:
  items: response.body
  filter: "item.status != 'decommissioned'"
  metrics:
    - name: example_device_up
      help: Device status (1 online, 0 otherwise)
      value: "item.status == 'online'"
      labels:
        serial: item.serial
        site_id: item.siteId
  info:
    - name: example_device_info
      labels:
        serial: item.serial
        model: item.model

Metrics are gauges or counters, and descriptive attributes go to _info metrics (value 1) rather than to every series. A sample carries the time the API gives when the mapping reads it, else the collection time. The mapping recipes show the common patterns.

items.title: Budget engine
items.text:
Every provider declares its limits:

Kind Example Enforced as rate 10 requests per second a token bucket: requests wait for a token concurrency 4 requests in flight requests wait for a free slot quota 10,000 calls per day, per month, or per rolling hour a counter per window: requests are refused once it is spent

A limit has a scope: one counter for the whole Tapyr instance, per account, per credential, per endpoint, or per value of a request variable such as an organization. Every request reserves its place in every limit that applies to it before leaving, retries, pages, token requests and discovery included: this is how Tapyr guarantees that it never exceeds a declared limit.

The engine also learns from the provider:

  • Quota headers. When the API announces its quota in response headers, Tapyr follows them: the real maximum (max: auto), what is left, and when the window resets. What the provider counts beyond Tapyr's own requests is the external usage, from another tool or a script using the same quota.
  • 429 responses. A 429 Too Many Requests puts its scope in penalty for its Retry-After, growing on repeated ones. An unexpected 429, one that no declared limit predicted, is counted apart: it means the definition misses a limit, or someone else shares it.
  • Retry reserve. 10% of every quota (settings.budget.retryReserve) is kept for retries, so that a burst of errors does not starve the rest of the day.

items.title: Planner
items.text:
Before running, and again while running, the planner checks that the jobs fit every quota. For each quota scope, it projects the calls of every job over the window: calls per run (from the run history, or the estimate of the template), times the instances of the fan-out, times the runs per window.

  • When the projection fits, every job runs at its desired interval.
  • When it does not, the planner stretches the intervals, lowest priority first: all the low jobs of the scope by a common factor, up to 12 times (settings.budget.maxStretch), then the normal ones, then high. The interval actually used is the effective interval.
  • critical jobs are never stretched. When they alone exceed a quota, the plan is infeasible: tapyr plan exits with code 3, and tapyr run starts anyway with a warning.
  • Every 15 minutes (settings.budget.replanInterval), and after a reload or an inventory change, the planner starts again from what is left in the window and from the pace of the external usage, so that a morning of retries tightens the afternoon instead of exhausting the quota.
  • Between two of these, when another client suddenly spends the same quota, or Tapyr needs more requests than planned, the current plan may no longer fit: Tapyr checks it at most once a minute and replans at once when it would exhaust a quota before the reset (settings.budget.replanOnProjection, on by default).

tapyr plan runs the same planner offline, before you deploy a configuration: see the getting started guide.

items.title: Failures
items.text:
Tapyr classifies every failed request:

  • Transient errors (network errors, timeouts, and the statuses the provider declares retryable, usually 5xx) are retried with exponential backoff and jitter, up to 4 attempts, within the deadline of the run. Only idempotent requests are retried.
  • Rate limited requests are retried after their penalty.
  • Authentication failures with a token (OAuth2, session login) drop the token and retry once with a new one. A rejected token or login request backs off from 1 minute up to 1 hour, so that a wrong password never locks an account.
  • Other client errors and responses that cannot be decoded fail the run without a retry.

After 5 consecutive transient failures, the circuit breaker of the account (or of the target) opens: Tapyr stops calling it and spends no quota, then probes again after a cooldown of 2 minutes, doubling up to 30 minutes. A run ends as success, partial, failed, or skipped (skipped_budget, skipped_circuit, skipped_overlap when the previous run is still going).

items.title: Series and outputs
items.text:
Tapyr keeps track of the series each job instance produced at its last successful run:

  • A series that disappears from the answer (a device removed) is stale: it leaves the Prometheus exposition, and push outputs receive a stale marker.
  • A failed run changes nothing: the series stay until staleAfter (3 times the effective interval by default), then go stale.
  • A sample whose source timestamp was already sent is dropped, since APIs often return overlapping windows.

Three output types deliver the samples: prometheus (served on /metrics for a scrape), remote_write (Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, Mimir, Thanos) and otlp (an OpenTelemetry Collector or any OTLP backend). Each push output has its own bounded queue: a slow backend never blocks the collection or the other outputs. Outputs has the details.

items.title: Self-observability
items.text:
Tapyr exposes its own metrics on /metrics/self: requests by status, retries and waits, the quotas used, left and projected, the effective intervals, the freshness of every job, circuits and outputs. They never carry identifiers such as serials or organization IDs. The other ways to see what it does:

  • /healthz and /readyz, for probes;
  • a read-only status API under /api/v1, described in /api/v1/openapi.yaml;
  • the read-only web UI on /ui/: overview, graph of providers, accounts, jobs and outputs, budgets with their timelines, the plan, and a live view of the raw responses when the debug endpoint is enabled;
  • the tapyr-overview Grafana dashboard and example alert rules.

items.title: State
items.text:
tapyr run keeps a SQLite database (settings.state.path, default ./data/tapyr.db), written every 5 seconds and on shutdown:

  • the consumption of every quota window, so that a restart does not forget what was already spent;
  • the cached inventories and the run history used by the planner;
  • the tokens of the providers, encrypted when TAPYR_STATE_KEY is set;
  • the series of every job instance and the last timestamps sent.

Losing it is not fatal, since the quota headers correct the counters, but keep it on persistent storage: see Operations.

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
In about ten minutes, with the tapyr binary alone, you will collect metrics from a simulated API, see how Tapyr plans the quota before spending it, and watch it adapt when the quota shrinks. No vendor account, no Docker: every provider package comes with a simulator built into the binary.

For the full demo with VictoriaMetrics and Grafana dashboards, see the demo compose instead.

items.title: 1. Install
items.text:
Download the archive of your platform from the releases page, or see Install for the image and the signature checks. Then:

tapyr version

items.title: 2. Write a configuration
items.text:
Start the simulator of example-sim, the example provider, in a terminal of its own. It serves a small API on 127.0.0.1:8081 with 3 sites, their networks and 5 devices, behind an API key, with paginated answers and a daily quota of 5000 calls:

tapyr sim --provider example-sim

In another terminal, create a directory and a file config.yaml in it:

apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
kind: Account
metadata:
  name: demo
spec:
  provider: example-sim
  secrets:
    apiKey: { env: TAPYR_EXAMPLE_API_KEY }
  labels:
    environment: lab
---
apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: devices
spec:
  account: demo
  template: example-sim-devices
  interval: 1m
  priority: critical
---
apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: network-devices
spec:
  account: demo
  template: example-sim-network-devices
---
apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
kind: Output
metadata:
  name: prometheus
spec:
  type: prometheus
  • The account connects to the provider. Its secret is a reference to an environment variable, never the value itself, and its labels are added to every sample.
  • The jobs use templates of the provider package: devices lists the devices every minute, at the critical priority. network-devices needs discovery: it runs once per network, and the networks are listed per site. You declare only the job you want; Tapyr runs the sites and the networks as implicit parent jobs.
  • The output serves the samples on /metrics, for Prometheus to scrape.

Concepts explains each piece.

items.title: 3. Check what it will spend
items.text:
validate checks the configuration; --check-secrets also checks that the secrets are there:

$ tapyr validate --config . --check-secrets
config.yaml:8:5: spec.secrets.apiKey: environment variable TAPYR_EXAMPLE_API_KEY is not set
configuration is invalid: 1 error

$ export TAPYR_EXAMPLE_API_KEY=sim-api-key
$ tapyr validate --config . --check-secrets
configuration is valid: 5 providers, 21 job templates, 1 account, 2 jobs, 1 output

plan projects the calls of every job against every quota, before a single request. Discovery has not run yet, so tell it how many instances to expect: 3 sites, and 5 networks in all.

$ tapyr plan --config . --fanout example-sim-sites=3 --fanout example-sim-networks=5
QUOTA SCOPE                      WINDOW       BUDGET         PROJECTED                   RESERVE  STATUS
example-sim/daily                24h          4500           4679                        500      INFEASIBLE (104.0%)
  account=demo
  job devices                    desired 1m   effective 1m   1440 runs x 3 pages = 4536
  job network-devices            desired 5m   effective 1h   24 runs x 5 x 1 page = 126  (stretched x12.00, priority normal, quota example-sim/daily account=demo)
  job demo.example-sim-networks  desired 30m  effective 6h   4 runs x 3 x 1 page = 13    (stretched x12.00, priority low, quota example-sim/daily account=demo)
  job demo.example-sim-sites     desired 1h   effective 12h  2 runs x 2 pages = 4        (stretched x12.00, priority low, quota example-sim/daily account=demo)

The plan is infeasible: critical jobs alone exceed a quota, or stretching every other job to the maximum is not enough.

Read it from the top. The daily quota is 5000 calls; 500 are kept in reserve for retries, which leaves a budget of 4500. Listing 5 devices takes 3 pages, so polling them every minute costs 4320 calls a day, 4536 with the 5% the planner adds for retries: more than the budget on its own. The planner stretched every other job 12 times, the most it allows, and it is still not enough. A critical job is never slowed down, so the plan is infeasible, and tapyr plan exits with code 3: a CI would have caught it before deployment.

Poll the devices every 2 minutes instead (interval: 2m in config.yaml) and plan again:

$ tapyr plan --config . --fanout example-sim-sites=3 --fanout example-sim-networks=5
QUOTA SCOPE                      WINDOW       BUDGET         PROJECTED                     RESERVE  STATUS
example-sim/daily                24h          4500           3982                          500      ok (88.5%)
  account=demo
  job devices                    desired 2m   effective 2m   720 runs x 3 pages = 2268
  job network-devices            desired 5m   effective 5m   288 runs x 5 x 1 page = 1512
  job demo.example-sim-networks  desired 30m  effective 30m  48 runs x 3 x 1 page = 151
  job demo.example-sim-sites     desired 1h   effective 1h   24 runs x 2 pages = 50

Every job now runs at the interval it asked for, within 89% of the budget.

items.title: 4. Run it
items.text:
The log lines below leave out their time stamp (ts=...).

$ tapyr run --config . --log-format text
level=INFO msg="collector started" component=run address=127.0.0.1:9790 instances=2 discovered_instances=0 outputs=1 ledger_entries=0
level=INFO msg="run finished" component=run provider=example-sim account=demo job=devices instance=devices run_id=000001 requests=3 retries=0 pages=3 items=5 samples=16 deduplicated=0 mapping_errors=0 truncated=false

The first runs are spread over the first 10% of their interval, so that a restart never fires every request at once: the devices come within seconds, the sites within 6 minutes. The instances that discovery finds run first within the same tenth of their interval: the networks of the 3 sites come within 3 minutes after the sites, and the devices of each network within 30 seconds after its network, so everything is there within about 10 minutes (under 5 in a test run). After their first run, the instances of a fan-out run at their own point of the interval, so that a thousand networks never fire at once. The Graph page of the UI shows the instances as they appear. A restart does not wait again: the inventory is cached. Tapyr keeps its state (quota consumption, inventories, run history) in ./data/tapyr.db, so that a restart remembers what was already spent today.

$ curl -s 127.0.0.1:9790/metrics | grep '^example_device_up'
example_device_up{environment="lab",serial="SIM-0001",site_id="site-a"} 1
example_device_up{environment="lab",serial="SIM-0002",site_id="site-a"} 0
example_device_up{environment="lab",serial="SIM-0003",site_id="site-b"} 1
example_device_up{environment="lab",serial="SIM-0004",site_id="site-b"} 1

items.title: 5. Look around
items.text:
Open the web UI on http://127.0.0.1:9790/ui/: the overview, the graph of the provider, account, jobs and output, every job with its runs, the budgets with their consumption over the day, and the plan. It is read-only: the configuration stays in your files.

Tapyr reports on itself on /metrics/self, and in a JSON status API under /api/v1:

$ curl -s 127.0.0.1:9790/metrics/self | grep -E '^tapyr_budget_(limit|used|remaining)\{'
tapyr_budget_limit{limit="daily",provider="example-sim",scope="account=demo"} 5000
tapyr_budget_remaining{limit="daily",provider="example-sim",scope="account=demo"} 4997
tapyr_budget_used{limit="daily",provider="example-sim",scope="account=demo"} 3

$ curl -s 127.0.0.1:9790/api/v1/jobs        # jobs, intervals, instances, last runs
$ curl -s 127.0.0.1:9790/api/v1/budgets     # every limit and scope

items.title: 6. Squeeze the quota
items.text:
Leave Tapyr running. Stop the simulator (Ctrl-C) and start it again with its quota-tight scenario, where the daily quota is only 600 calls:

tapyr sim --provider example-sim --scenario quota-tight

The provider declares its daily quota as max: auto: Tapyr takes the real maximum from the quota headers of every response. At the next run of devices, it learns that the quota is now 600, and the planner replans at once, spreading what is left of the quota over what is left of the day until the reset at midnight UTC. Until about 18:00 UTC, there is too much day left for 600 calls, and you see this:

level=INFO msg="effective interval changed" component=planner provider=example-sim account=demo job=demo.example-sim-sites desired=1h0m0s previous=1h0m0s effective=12h0m0s reason="quota example-sim/daily account=demo"
level=INFO msg="effective interval changed" component=planner provider=example-sim account=demo job=demo.example-sim-networks desired=30m0s previous=30m0s effective=6h0m0s reason="quota example-sim/daily account=demo"
level=WARN msg="plan infeasible: critical jobs alone exceed the remaining quota" component=planner limit=example-sim/daily scope="account=demo" budget=523 projected=1056.3525101437106

Later in the day, what is left of the 600 calls is enough for the few hours before the reset: Tapyr learns the new limit (tapyr_budget_limit drops to 600, the Budgets page shows it) and keeps every interval, which is the right decision. The rest of this step needs more than about 6 hours before midnight UTC.

The low-priority discovery jobs are stretched 12 times. devices keeps running every 2 minutes, because a critical job is never slowed down: at this pace, it would spend the rest of the quota before the daily reset, and every request after that would be refused until midnight UTC. The Overview page of the UI shows the warning, and the Budgets page the new limit.

Whether polling the devices every 2 minutes is worth the quota is your decision, not Tapyr's: say so with the priority. Set priority: high on devices in config.yaml, and reload the configuration without stopping Tapyr:

kill -HUP "$(pgrep -f 'tapyr run')"

(pgrep comes with procps, missing from minimal systems: kill -HUP with the process ID of tapyr run does the same.)

level=INFO msg="effective interval changed" component=planner provider=example-sim account=demo job=devices desired=2m0s previous=2m0s effective=4m6s reason="quota example-sim/daily account=demo"
level=INFO msg="configuration reloaded" component=run instances=10 discovered_instances=8 retired_instances=0 outputs=1

The plan is feasible again: devices now runs every 4 minutes or so, which fits what is left of the quota until the reset. The exact figures depend on the time left before midnight UTC, since the planner replans from the remaining budget and the remaining time. When the quota resets, or when you restart the simulator without the scenario, the intervals come back to the ones you asked for.

Stop Tapyr and the simulator with Ctrl-C when you are done; ./data holds the state of this guide and can be deleted.

items.title: 7. Next steps
items.text:
• A real provider. Pick a package among the providers: its README lists the credentials it needs (read-only keys are enough, Tapyr never writes), what it collects and its limits. Replace the account of this guide with one for that provider, run tapyr validate --check-secrets and tapyr plan, then tapyr run.
  • A time series database. Scrape /metrics with Prometheus, or push with a remote_write or otlp output: see Outputs.
  • Dashboards and alerts. Every package ships a Grafana dashboard, and Tapyr ships one of its own with alert rules.
  • Deploy. Install covers the image, systemd and Kubernetes; Operations covers the state store, reloads, monitoring and security.
  • Every field. The configuration reference.

items.title: Install
items.text: Tapyr is a single static binary with the web UI embedded. Releases ship it for Linux, macOS and Windows (amd64, arm64), and as the multi-arch image ghcr.io/kentrow/tapyr.

items.title: Binary
items.text:
Download the archive of your platform and checksums.txt from the releases page, check it, then put tapyr in your PATH. On Linux:

VERSION=0.4.0
ARCH=$(uname -m | sed 's/x86_64/amd64/; s/aarch64/arm64/')
curl -LO https://github.com/kentrow/tapyr/releases/download/v$VERSION/tapyr_${VERSION}_linux_${ARCH}.tar.gz
curl -LO https://github.com/kentrow/tapyr/releases/download/v$VERSION/checksums.txt
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c checksums.txt
tar xzf tapyr_${VERSION}_linux_${ARCH}.tar.gz tapyr
./tapyr version

The archives are tapyr_<version>_<os>_<arch>: linux, darwin or windows (a .zip), amd64 or arm64. On macOS, sha256sum is not installed: check the archive with shasum -a 256 --ignore-missing -c checksums.txt.

Each archive has its SBOM next to it (<archive>.sbom.json, SPDX), and holds LICENSE, NOTICE and THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES, the licenses and notices of the software the binary includes.

items.title: Homebrew
items.text:
From v0.2.1, on macOS:

brew install kentrow/tap/tapyr
brew trust kentrow/tap            # once, so that a plain `brew upgrade` includes it

The binary is not notarized by Apple: the cask removes its quarantine attribute at install, otherwise macOS would refuse to run it. To check what you run, verify the signatures of the release first.

items.title: deb and rpm packages
items.text:
From v0.2.1, every release has .deb and .rpm packages for amd64 and arm64: the binary in /usr/bin, the hardened systemd unit and an example in /etc/tapyr. They are static, without dependencies, and covered by the checksums, their signature and the provenance below.

VERSION=0.4.0
ARCH=$(dpkg --print-architecture)    # or: uname -m | sed 's/x86_64/amd64/; s/aarch64/arm64/'
curl -LO https://github.com/kentrow/tapyr/releases/download/v$VERSION/tapyr_${VERSION}_linux_${ARCH}.deb    # or .rpm
curl -LO https://github.com/kentrow/tapyr/releases/download/v$VERSION/checksums.txt
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c checksums.txt
sudo dpkg -i tapyr_${VERSION}_linux_${ARCH}.deb                                                             # or: sudo rpm -i ...

The service does not start by itself: without a configuration, it would collect nothing. Write /etc/tapyr/config.yaml from config.yaml.example, the secrets in /etc/tapyr/tapyr.env (mode 0600), then sudo systemctl enable --now tapyr. The systemd guide covers how to run it.

An upgrade restarts the service if it runs, and keeps the state store. A removal, even a purge, keeps /etc/tapyr and the state store in /var/lib/private/tapyr: it remembers the quotas already spent and the rotated tokens. Delete them by hand if you really mean to.

items.title: Container image
items.text:
docker run -d --name tapyr \
  -v "$PWD/config:/etc/tapyr:ro" \
  -v tapyr-data:/home/nonroot/data \
  -p 9790:9790 \
  ghcr.io/kentrow/tapyr:0.4.0
  • The image runs tapyr run --config /etc/tapyr as the nonroot user (uid 65532), on gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12.
  • The state store (quota consumption, rotated tokens, counters) defaults to ./data/tapyr.db, that is /home/nonroot/data in the image: keep it on a volume, or Tapyr forgets on restart what it already spent of the daily and monthly quotas.
  • Set settings.server.listen to 0.0.0.0:9790 in the configuration, so that the published port reaches the UI, the status API and /metrics.
  • Secrets come from environment variables or files ({ env: NAME }, { file: /path }): pass them with -e or mount them, never in the configuration files.
  • docker kill -s HUP tapyr reloads the configuration.

Tags: X.Y.Z, X.Y (latest patch of a minor version) and latest (latest release). A release candidate has its tag X.Y.Z-rc.N only.

items.title: systemd
items.text: The deb and rpm packages install it. For a binary installed by hand, examples/systemd has a hardened unit: a dynamic user, the configuration in /etc/tapyr, the secrets in an environment file read by systemd, the state store in /var/lib/tapyr, and systemctl reload tapyr for a reload.

items.title: Kubernetes
items.text:
The Helm chart is published with every release, signed:

kubectl create namespace tapyr
kubectl -n tapyr create secret generic tapyr --from-env-file=tapyr.env
helm install tapyr oci://ghcr.io/kentrow/charts/tapyr --namespace tapyr --values my-values.yaml

Without Helm, examples/kubernetes has Kustomize manifests: a Deployment of one replica (non-root, read-only root file system, probes on /readyz and /healthz), its Service, a volume for the state store, and the configuration as a ConfigMap whose changes roll the Deployment out. Run a single replica: a second one would spend the same quotas without coordinating.

items.title: Verify the signatures
items.text:
The checksums and the image are signed with cosign in keyless mode by the release workflow of the repository. The signature proves that the files and the image were built by that workflow, from a tag of Kentrow/tapyr. The identity is compared as written, case included.

# The checksums of a release (then check the archives with sha256sum, above).
cosign verify-blob checksums.txt \
  --bundle checksums.txt.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity "https://github.com/Kentrow/tapyr/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v$VERSION" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

# The image.
cosign verify ghcr.io/kentrow/tapyr:$VERSION \
  --certificate-identity "https://github.com/Kentrow/tapyr/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v$VERSION" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

The Helm chart, from v0.2.1:

cosign verify ghcr.io/kentrow/charts/tapyr:$VERSION \
  --certificate-identity "https://github.com/Kentrow/tapyr/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v$VERSION" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

The SBOM of the image is attached to it as an attestation:

docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/kentrow/tapyr:$VERSION --format '{{ json .SBOM }}'

items.title: Verify the provenance
items.text:
From v0.1.1, every archive and the image carry their SLSA build provenance, as GitHub artifact attestations: the workflow that built them, from which commit and tag, on which runner. The GitHub CLI verifies them, and the options below make it refuse anything not built by the release workflow from the tag of the version:

# An archive.
gh attestation verify "tapyr_${VERSION}_linux_amd64.tar.gz" --repo Kentrow/tapyr \
  --signer-workflow Kentrow/tapyr/.github/workflows/release.yml \
  --source-ref "refs/tags/v$VERSION" --deny-self-hosted-runners

# The image.
gh attestation verify "oci://ghcr.io/kentrow/tapyr:$VERSION" --repo Kentrow/tapyr \
  --signer-workflow Kentrow/tapyr/.github/workflows/release.yml \
  --source-ref "refs/tags/v$VERSION" --deny-self-hosted-runners

# The Helm chart, from v0.2.1.
gh attestation verify "oci://ghcr.io/kentrow/charts/tapyr:$VERSION" --repo Kentrow/tapyr \
  --signer-workflow Kentrow/tapyr/.github/workflows/release.yml \
  --source-ref "refs/tags/v$VERSION" --deny-self-hosted-runners

The attestations of the archives are also a release asset, tapyr_${VERSION}_provenance.intoto.jsonl, to verify without the attestations API of GitHub: add --bundle tapyr_${VERSION}_provenance.intoto.jsonl to the command of an archive. For the image, --bundle-from-oci reads the attestation stored next to it in the registry.

items.title: From source
items.text:
Go 1.27 and Node.js 22.12 or later (Vite 8 needs it):

git clone https://github.com/kentrow/tapyr.git
cd tapyr
make build        # the UI, then the static binary in ./bin/tapyr
make docker       # or the image tapyr:dev

items.title: Operations
items.text: What to know to run Tapyr for real: where it keeps its state, how to change its configuration, how to watch it and how to expose it safely. Install covers the binary, the image, the systemd unit and the Kubernetes manifests.

items.title: One instance per set of accounts
items.text:
Run a single tapyr run for a given set of accounts. Two instances polling the same accounts do not coordinate: each one spends the whole quota it was given, and together they exceed it. On Kubernetes, keep one replica with the Recreate strategy, as the example manifests do.

When another tool must keep using the same credentials, give Tapyr its part with budget.share on the account (0.5 for half of every quota). Tapyr also measures what others consume through the quota headers, when the provider sends them, and slows down accordingly; budget.share makes the split explicit.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
--config takes files or directories, and can be repeated (TAPYR_CONFIG in the environment, paths separated like in PATH: : on Linux and macOS). In a directory, Tapyr reads the *.yaml and *.yml files of the directory and its subdirectories, sorted by path, and skips hidden files and directories; a file can hold several documents separated by ---. Relative paths in a document (a secret file, a CA bundle, providerPaths, the state path) are resolved against the file that declares them.

Before applying a change, check it:

tapyr validate --config /etc/tapyr --check-secrets   # exit code 2 when invalid
tapyr plan --config /etc/tapyr                        # exit code 3 when infeasible

Keep the configuration in Git, and run both commands in the CI of that repository: tapyr plan turns "this change would exhaust the daily quota at 3 pm" into a failed check instead of an incident.

items.title: Reload
items.text:
SIGHUP reloads the configuration without a restart (systemctl reload tapyr, docker kill -s HUP tapyr, or a rollout on Kubernetes, where the example ConfigMap is hashed):

  • The new configuration is loaded and validated first. When it is invalid, the reload is rejected, the error is logged (configuration reload rejected) and the running configuration keeps going; tapyr_config_last_reload_success drops to 0.
  • Otherwise the running jobs finish, the consumption of every quota carries over, unchanged instances keep their schedule, and the series of removed jobs go stale.
  • Changes to server (except server.debug, applied on reload), state.path and log need a restart; Tapyr logs a warning when a reload contains one.

items.title: Secrets
items.text: Secrets are references, never values: { env: NAME } for an environment variable, { file: /path } for a file (a Docker or Kubernetes secret, a systemd credential). Tapyr redacts their values, and the tokens it obtains, from its logs, errors, status API and debug output. A secret shorter than 4 characters cannot be redacted reliably and is reported at startup.

items.title: State store
items.text:
The state store is a SQLite database, settings.state.path (default ./data/tapyr.db, relative to the working directory; /home/nonroot/data/tapyr.db in the image). It holds:

Data Why it matters Quota consumption per window Without it, a restart forgets what was already spent today or this month, and the first requests may hit a quota the provider still counts Tokens and rotated refresh tokens Some providers rotate them at every refresh (Aruba Central): losing the store means bootstrapping new credentials Inventories and run history Discovery restarts from the cache instead of waiting for its parents; the planner estimates from real runs Series and last timestamps sent Stale markers and deduplication work across restarts

Keep it on persistent storage (a volume, StateDirectory= with systemd), and back it up with the host. Do not delete it to "reset" Tapyr. It is written every 5 seconds and on shutdown; tapyr_state_flush_failures_total counts failed writes (full disk, permissions).

Set TAPYR_STATE_KEY to encrypt the tokens in the store (AES-GCM, with a key derived from its value). Without it, Tapyr logs a warning once and stores them in clear. Changing the key makes the stored tokens unreadable: they are requested again, except for rotated tokens that need a new bootstrap.

items.title: Monitoring Tapyr
items.text:
Tapyr exposes its own metrics on /metrics/self. Scrape them with honor_labels: true, since they carry the job label of the Tapyr job:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: tapyr
    metrics_path: /metrics/self
    honor_labels: true
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["tapyr:9790"]

Where nothing scrapes Tapyr, settings.selfMetrics.outputs pushes them through an output instead, every 30 seconds.

  • Dashboard. dashboards/tapyr-overview.json (Grafana): health, quotas left and projected, job freshness and intervals, provider calls, outputs. Every provider package ships a dashboard of the data it collects as well.
  • Alerts. examples/alerts/tapyr-alerts.yaml has 14 rules for Prometheus or vmalert, explained in Alerts: process down, stale jobs, open circuits, re-authentication required, quotas about to run out, unexpected 429s, outputs dropping samples, rejected reloads, state store failures.
  • Probes. /healthz answers 503 when the internal loops are stuck (liveness); /readyz answers 503 until the configuration is loaded, the state store answers and every output has started (readiness). Neither is ever protected by basic auth.
  • Logs. JSON on stderr by default, with component, provider, account, job and run_id fields; --log-format text (or TAPYR_LOG_FORMAT, or settings.log.format) for plain lines. Requests are logged at debug level only; repetitive warnings are logged at most once per minute.

items.title: Exposing the server
items.text:
Tapyr listens on 127.0.0.1:9790 by default. To reach it from another host or from outside a container, set settings.server.listen: 0.0.0.0:9790. The UI and the status API show your infrastructure (accounts, endpoints, inventories, errors): protect them before exposing them.

apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
kind: Settings
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  server:
    listen: 0.0.0.0:9790
    basicAuth:
      username: { env: TAPYR_UI_USER }
      password: { env: TAPYR_UI_PASSWORD }
      protectMetrics: false     # true also protects /metrics and /metrics/self
  • Basic auth protects /api and /ui, and the metrics with protectMetrics. Prometheus then needs the same credentials (basic_auth in the scrape configuration).
  • TLS. A reverse proxy is the recommended way to terminate TLS. settings.server.tls (certFile, keyFile) serves HTTPS directly.
  • Debug endpoint. settings.server.debug.enabled keeps the last raw responses of every job, redacted and truncated to 1 MiB, for the Live debug page and /api/v1/debug/.... It helps writing and fixing mappings; turn it off when you do not need it, since the payloads describe your devices.

items.title: Upgrading
items.text:
Releases follow Semantic Versioning. Before 1.0, a minor version (0.2.0) may change the configuration format, with a new apiVersion and the migration in the changelog; a patch version (0.1.1) never does. To upgrade:

  1. Read the changelog between your version and the new one.
  2. Run tapyr validate and tapyr plan of the new version on your configuration.
  3. Replace the binary or the image tag, keep the state store, restart.

Pin the image to a version (ghcr.io/kentrow/tapyr:0.4.0, or 0.4 for the patches of a minor version) rather than latest, and verify its signature.

items.title: Capacity
items.text:
• Outputs. Each push output has a queue of capacity samples. Size it for the backend outage you want to ride out: samples per minute across your jobs, times the minutes (see Sizing the queue).
  • Concurrency. settings.collection.maxConcurrentRequests (default 32) bounds the requests in flight across all providers; the concurrency limits of the providers apply on top of it.
  • Runaway discovery. forEach.maxInstances (default 10000) caps the instances of a fan-out, and settings.mapping caps the items and samples of a run and the cost of CEL expressions.

items.title: Outputs
items.text:
Tapyr sends what it collects through Output documents. A job sends to every output, or to the outputs listed in its spec.outputs. Each output has its own queue: a slow or unavailable backend never blocks collection or the other outputs.

Type Protocol Typical backends prometheus Pull, served on /metrics Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics vmagent, Grafana Alloy, any scraper remote_write Prometheus remote write 1.0 (protobuf, snappy) Prometheus (remote write receiver enabled), VictoriaMetrics, Grafana Mimir, Thanos Receive, Cortex otlp OTLP metrics over HTTP (protobuf) or gRPC OpenTelemetry Collector, any OTLP receiver

items.title: prometheus
items.text:
apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
kind: Output
metadata: { name: prom }
spec:
  type: prometheus
  prometheus:
    exposeTimestamps: false   # the default, as recommended by Prometheus

/metrics holds the samples of the last successful run of every job instance. A series that a run no longer produces leaves the exposition at once; the series of a failing instance stay until staleAfter (3x the effective interval by default). The exposition is served in the Prometheus text format or OpenMetrics, by content negotiation, and gzip-compressed for the scrapers that accept it (all the usual ones do). At most one prometheus output may be configured.

items.title: remote_write
items.text:
apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
kind: Output
metadata: { name: victoria }
spec:
  type: remote_write
  remoteWrite:
    url: http://victoriametrics:8428/api/v1/write
    headers: { X-Scope-OrgID: tenant-1 }            # literals or { env: ... } / { file: ... } secrets
    basicAuth: { username: { env: VM_USER }, password: { env: VM_PASSWORD } }
    timeout: 10s
  queue:
    capacity: 50000        # samples; the oldest are dropped when full
    maxBatch: 5000         # samples per request
    flushInterval: 5s      # a partial batch leaves after this delay
  externalLabels:
    tapyr_instance: lab    # added to every sample that does not set the label
  • Samples carry their timestamp: the source timestamp when the mapping sets one, else the time the response was received.
  • A series that goes away (absent from the next successful run, its job instance removed by discovery or a reload, or withdrawn after staleAfter) receives one staleness marker, so that queries stop returning it at once instead of after the lookback delta.
  • Samples whose source timestamp was already sent for the same series are not sent again (APIs often return overlapping windows); see tapyr_samples_deduplicated_total.
  • Metric metadata (type, help, unit) is sent on the first request and every minute.
  • Network errors, 5xx and 429 are retried with exponential backoff (1 second doubling up to 1 minute), honoring Retry-After. Other 4xx drop the batch, except a batch refused for out-of-order samples (below).

items.title: Series of slow jobs
items.text: A push output sends a sample of a series when its job runs, while a scraped exposition (prometheus) shows the last value at every scrape. Prometheus and VictoriaMetrics answer a query with the last sample of the previous 5 minutes (the lookback delta): the series of a job that runs every 15 minutes or every hour drop out of instant queries and graphs between two runs. Read them with last_over_time(metric[window]), the window two to three times the job interval, as the built-in dashboards do (dashboard conventions). A series that goes away stays visible for that window.

items.title: Out-of-order samples
items.text:
Source timestamps can be older than samples already ingested for a series, for example after a restart, when a job interval changes or when an API reports late data. They can also be older than what the backend still accepts at all: Prometheus refuses samples older than its in-memory head (about an hour) as "out of bounds", even on a fresh server, so any API reporting a timestamp of the day before hits it.

Prometheus rejects such samples unless out-of-order ingestion is enabled, with a window longer than the age of the oldest source timestamp:

# prometheus.yml
storage:
  tsdb:
    out_of_order_time_window: 7d

Without it, one sample out of bounds makes Prometheus refuse the whole request (400), over remote write and OTLP alike, and it ingests none of its samples. Tapyr then splits the batch: it sends both halves again, one after the other, and splits a refused half further, down to the samples really refused. The other samples of the batch, the fresh ones of the other jobs included, arrive, in order. A batch costs a few more requests to the backend (about two per halving, 13 halvings at most for the default maxBatch of 5000), never API quota. Splitting stops after 64 requests for one batch: the halves left are sent once more each, and dropped if refused.

The samples refused are counted in tapyr_output_samples_dropped_total{reason="out_of_order"}, and logged as samples dropped: the backend rejected the batch with class=out_of_order; every refused request counts in tapyr_output_send_failures_total{class="out_of_order"}. Mimir and Thanos have settings equivalent to the out-of-order window; VictoriaMetrics accepts such samples.

items.title: otlp
items.text:
apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
kind: Output
metadata: { name: collector }
spec:
  type: otlp
  otlp:
    endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318   # /v1/metrics is added when the URL has no path
    protocol: http/protobuf                # or grpc (endpoint http://otel-collector:4317)
    headers: { api-key: { env: OTLP_API_KEY } }
    resourceAttributes: { deployment.environment: production }
    timeout: 10s
  queue: { capacity: 50000, maxBatch: 5000, flushInterval: 5s }
  • Payloads are built with the OTLP data model directly, not with the OpenTelemetry metrics SDK, so that points keep their source timestamps.
  • One resource per provider and account, with service.name=tapyr, service.instance.id (a random identifier kept in the state store, stable across restarts), tapyr.provider, tapyr.account and the configured resourceAttributes. The instrumentation scope is github.com/kentrow/tapyr.
  • Gauges map to OTLP gauges; counters to cumulative monotonic sums whose start time is the first time the output saw the series (a restart starts them again, which receivers treat as a reset).
  • A series that goes away receives one data point flagged FLAG_NO_RECORDED_VALUE.
  • Partial success responses count the rejected points; 429, 502, 503, 504 (HTTP) and UNAVAILABLE or RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED with RetryInfo (gRPC) are retried, honoring the delay asked by the receiver.
  • https:// endpoints use TLS with the system roots.

items.title: Sending less to an output
items.text:
spec.processing filters what an output receives, for that output only: a hosted backend billed by series can get less than a local one, without changing the provider packages. The rules are those of Prometheus metric_relabel_configs, so rules written for Prometheus carry over:

apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
kind: Output
metadata: { name: hosted }
spec:
  type: remote_write
  remoteWrite: { url: https://metrics.example.com/api/v1/write }
  processing:
    # No uplink metrics for this backend.
    - action: drop
      sourceLabels: [__name__]
      regex: "meraki_uplink_.*"
    # No access point metrics for the lab site.
    - action: drop
      sourceLabels: [__name__, site]
      regex: "aruba_ap_.*;lab"
    # No firmware label.
    - action: labeldrop
      regex: firmware
Action Keeps or drops keep, drop the samples whose sourceLabels values, joined by separator (;), match regex (__name__ is the metric name) labelkeep, labeldrop the labels whose name matches regex (never __name__)
  • The regex matches the whole value (it is anchored), in the RE2 syntax.
  • Samples removed by keep and drop are counted in tapyr_output_samples_filtered_total, not as dropped samples: filtering is what you asked for.
  • A labeldrop can make two series identical; the duplicates are dropped and counted in tapyr_output_samples_dropped_total{reason="duplicate"}, which the TapyrOutputDropping alert reports: remove a label only when the others still tell the series apart.
  • A changed rule applies from the next run of each job instance; the series it removes or renames get a stale marker then.
  • Tapyr's self-metrics are never filtered.

items.title: Sizing the queue
items.text: The queue holds capacity samples per output. While a backend is down, the batch at the head of the queue is retried and new samples queue behind it; once full, the oldest samples are dropped and counted. Size capacity for the outage you want to ride out: samples per minute across your jobs, times the minutes. The batch being sent is never dropped while its request is in flight.

items.title: Self-metrics to watch
items.text:
Metric Meaning tapyr_output_queue_samples Samples waiting; grows while a backend is slow or down tapyr_output_samples_sent_total Samples accepted by the backend tapyr_output_samples_dropped_total{reason} queue_full, rejected, out_of_order or duplicate (made identical by processing rules) tapyr_output_samples_filtered_total Samples removed by the keep and drop processing rules tapyr_output_send_failures_total{class} Failed requests: transient, throttled, rejected, out_of_order tapyr_output_last_success_timestamp_seconds Last successful send

settings.selfMetrics.outputs pushes Tapyr's own metrics through outputs too, every settings.selfMetrics.interval (30 seconds by default), for setups where nothing scrapes /metrics/self.

items.title: Testing against real backends
items.text: make integration starts VictoriaMetrics, an OpenTelemetry Collector and Prometheus with Docker Compose (test/integration/compose.yaml) and checks that samples and staleness markers land in all of them: remote write to VictoriaMetrics and Prometheus, OTLP/HTTP and OTLP/gRPC to the collector, OTLP to Prometheus, and the scrape of /metrics and /metrics/self (with honor_labels: true) by Prometheus. The Prometheus of the test enables out-of-order ingestion, since the simulator fixtures carry fixed source timestamps; a second one, without out-of-order window, receives remote write and OTLP too, and the test checks that it gets every sample stamped with the collection time while it refuses the samples with old source timestamps.

items.title: Provider ideas
items.text:
Candidate provider packages, with the rate-limit pattern each one would exercise. Networks are the first use case of Tapyr, not its boundary (ADR 0011): any metric-oriented API whose quota is worth planning can become a package.

This is a pool of ideas, not a commitment, and contributions are welcome: read Provider packages first. The limits below were gathered from public documentation in November 2026: verify them before writing a package, and cite their sources in the package. A provider that needs one of the engine gaps starts with an issue, since the engine changes first.

items.title: Network and SD-WAN (first use case)
items.text:
Juniper Mist and Cisco ThousandEyes, ideas of this page, are built-in packages since v0.3.0: juniper-mist and cisco-thousandeyes. UniFi Site Manager is one too: unifi-site-manager.

Provider Metrics of interest Limit pattern Notes VeloCloud Orchestrator SD-WAN links, QoE, failovers Verify Peplink InControl2, Cradlepoint NetCloud 4G/5G routers, signal, data usage Verify Same family as Teltonika EfficientIP SOLIDserver, Infoblox DHCP scope usage, subnet saturation, DNS health Verify (often on-prem, per-appliance) High-value, rarely exposed metrics Aruba Central (new, GreenLake) Same as classic Verify Planned separately from aruba-central-classic

items.title: Security and reputation
items.text: Provider Metrics of interest Limit pattern Notes VirusTotal Reputation of own IPs/domains Three simultaneous quotas: per minute, per day (reset 00:00 UTC), per month (reset 00:00 UTC on the 1st); v2 signals exhaustion with 204, v3 with 429 Multi-window quotas exist; v2 needs rate limiting signaled by a 204 Shodan Exposure of own IP ranges Monthly query credits Needs a request cost (credits) AbuseIPDB Reports on own IPs Daily checks quota

items.title: Internet measurement
items.text: Provider Metrics of interest Limit pattern Notes RIPE Atlas Latency, traceroutes, DNS from probes Credits per measurement, daily spending cap Needs a request cost (credits) RIPEstat, PeeringDB, Cloudflare Radar Prefix visibility, routing, Internet health Fair-use or per-minute limits, verify

items.title: Cloud, costs and AI
items.text: Provider Metrics of interest Limit pattern Notes AWS Cost Explorer Spend by service, account, tag Each request is billed Needs a request cost, in currency Microsoft Graph, Azure Resource Graph Intune compliance, Entra sign-ins, resources Throttling with Retry-After, per-tenant and per-app limits OVHcloud, Scaleway Consumption, invoices, quotas Verify LLM usage APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic admin APIs, LiteLLM) Tokens, spend per key or team Verify Very topical

items.title: Developer and SaaS
items.text: Provider Metrics of interest Limit pattern Notes GitHub Actions runs and durations, PRs, security alerts REST hourly budget; GraphQL points budget with variable cost per query (returned in the response) GraphQL needs a request cost settled from the response GitLab Pipeline durations, runner queues Per-user and per-IP limits, verify Okta, Entra ID Failed sign-ins, MFA Per-endpoint limits with X-Rate-Limit-* headers

items.title: Energy, home, sport (homelab showcase)
items.text: Provider Metrics of interest Limit pattern Notes Enphase Solar production, consumption Free plan: 10 hits/min and 1000 hits/month Tight monthly quota SolarEdge Solar production 300 requests/day Tight daily quota Netatmo Weather, indoor air quality Per-user and per-app limits, verify OpenWeatherMap Weather Per-minute and monthly limits depending on plan, verify Strava Activities, training load Read: 100 per 15 min (reset at :00, :15, :30, :45) and 1000 per day (reset at midnight UTC); both values packed in one header (X-ReadRateLimit-Usage: 15min,daily) Needs 15-minute aligned windows and quota sync from expressions

items.title: Engine gaps
items.text:
Most of the APIs above fit the configuration model as it is: rate, concurrency, calendar and rolling quota windows, scopes, header sync and Retry-After (04-budget-engine.md). Four mechanisms are missing. Each one is a generic, configurable feature, designed in its own issue before any package needs it:

Gap Today Needed by Request cost A quota counts one unit per request GitHub GraphQL (points per query, returned in the response), RIPE Atlas (credits per measurement), AWS Cost Explorer (every request is billed), Shodan (query credits) Quota windows aligned on any duration A fixed window is a calendar period (minute, hour, day, week, month) Strava (15 minutes, reset at :00, :15, :30 and :45) Quota sync from expressions The limit, the remaining and the reset come from one header each Strava (two windows packed in one header), APIs that report their quota in the body Rate limiting signaled other than by a status errors.rateLimited matches HTTP statuses VirusTotal v2 (204 without a body), APIs answering 200 with an error object

Windows that start at the first request (ThousandEyes) are not a gap when the API sends a reset header: every response sets the end of the window to the provider's (04-budget-engine.md, Header sync). They would be one for an API that sends none.

items.title: Sources
items.text:
• Strava rate limits: https://developers.strava.com/docs/rate-limits/
  • VirusTotal consumption quotas: https://docs.virustotal.com/docs/consumption-quotas-handled
  • Enphase developer plans: https://developer-v4.enphase.com/developer-plans
  • SolarEdge daily limit (as documented by Home Assistant): https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/solaredge

items.title: Provider packages
items.text: A provider package holds everything Tapyr knows about an API: the Provider (base URL, auth, pagination, limits, errors), job templates, a simulator, scenarios, a contract test, a dashboard and examples. Packages are declarative: YAML and CEL, no Go, except for the rare auth flows written as plugins. The layout is described in 03-configuration.md.

items.title: Built-in packages
items.text:
Package API Tier Validation aruba-central-classic HPE Aruba Networking Central (classic platform) REST API Official Real platform (Central classic API Gateway, 2026-11-10) and simulator cisco-thousandeyes Cisco ThousandEyes API v7 (tests, agents, network results) Official Simulator only example-sim Vendor-neutral example API, served by tapyr sim, for development, tests and demos Official Simulator only juniper-mist Juniper Mist cloud REST API (access points, switches, WAN edge) Official Simulator only meraki-dashboard Cisco Meraki Dashboard API v1 Official Real platform (Dashboard API v1, 2026-11-07) and simulator teltonika-rms Teltonika Remote Management System (RMS) cloud API Official Real platform (RMS API v3-BETA, 2026-11) and simulator teltonika-rutos Local REST API of Teltonika routers running RutOS 07.06 or later Official Real platform (RutOS 07.24.5, 2026-11) and simulator unifi-site-manager UniFi Site Manager API v1 (the consoles, sites, devices and ISP metrics of every console of a UI account) Official Real platform (Site Manager API 1.0.0, 2026-11-13) and simulator

tapyr provider list lists them with the packages of providerPaths, which override built-in packages of the same name; --output json adds their catalog metadata, templates and limits (provider catalog output).

Looking for an API to package? Provider ideas lists candidates in other domains, with their rate-limit patterns and the engine features some of them still need.

items.title: Writing a package
items.text:
1. Read the vendor documentation and write provider.yaml. Every limit cites its source in its source (vendor-docs with the link, measured with the date, or assumed), and in its description and the README for humans. The metadata describes the package in the catalog: displayName, categories from providers/categories.yaml, maintainers (GitHub handles), tier (official or community) and validation (simulator, or real-platform with a date and the platform version), see 03-configuration.md. Prefer endpoints that return many objects per request (organization-wide lists, large pages): the budget engine spends quota deliberately, the templates should too.
  2. Write the job templates (templates/*.yaml) with estimate.pagesPerRun. Metric names follow <prefix>_<object>_<measure>_<unit> in base units, descriptive attributes go to _info metrics, and no high-cardinality label (client MAC addresses, IPs) is used.
  3. Build the simulator (sim/sim.yaml): a synthetic inventory with template fixtures (see 08-simulator.md), or static fixtures from a recording. Ship the default, quota-tight and bad-day scenarios.
  4. Write the contract test (tests/contract.yaml, tests/contract.env) and generate tests/expected.prom with tapyr provider lint --update <dir>. Review the samples: they are the contract of the package.
  5. Add a Grafana dashboard (dashboards/*.json, with a datasource variable, an API quota row when the API has a quota, and a link to Tapyr / Overview, following the dashboard conventions), examples (examples/*.yaml) and the README. Every package README follows the same skeleton, as in example-sim:
  6. an introduction (the API, what is collected) with the Validation status (real platform or simulator, versions, dates);
  7. Requirements, when there are (firmware versions, permissions, network access);
  8. Coverage: a table Template | Endpoint | Default interval | Requests | Metrics (requests per run), then the labels, joins and conversions;
  9. Auth setup: how to get the credentials and give them to Tapyr;
  10. Limits: a table Limit | Value | Source, then the quota maths with the default intervals;
  11. Simulator: the command, with the port the simulator gets under tapyr sim --all --listen-base 127.0.0.1:8081 (8081 plus its portOffset), the credentials it accepts and a Scenario | Effect table;
  12. Dashboard, Known caveats, and End-to-end test when there is one.
  13. tapyr provider lint --catalog <dir> must pass.

items.title: Dashboard conventions
items.text:
The dashboards of the packages and Tapyr / Overview read the same way, whatever the API:

  • Colors carry a meaning. Grafana's named colors (green, orange, red, blue, text), so that the dashboards follow the theme of each Grafana:
  • a count of problems (devices down, failed runs) is green at 0, then red from 1 when it needs action, or orange when it is a warning (alerting devices, a backup uplink, a device not seen for an hour);
  • a count or a measure with no good or bad value (devices, clients, uptime) is text, never the default thresholds of Grafana (red from 80);
  • the share of a quota left is red under 10%, orange under 25%, green above;
  • quota charts draw the limit in dashed red, Tapyr in blue and other clients in orange;
  • status codes: 2xx green, 429 orange, other errors red.
  • States are state timelines. A 0/1 metric (an interface up, an uplink active) is a state timeline with value mappings (Up/Down), not a line between 0 and 1.
  • Thresholds come from a source. Mobile signal (RSRP, RSRQ, SINR, RSSI) uses the categories of the Teltonika recommendations as dashed lines; resource use (memory, flash) is orange from 80% and red from 90%. A measure without a sound threshold (temperatures, load) has none.
  • Rankings are bars. "The 10 busiest access points" is a bar gauge of the current values, not ten lines that change members over time.
  • Empty is an answer. A panel that can have nothing to show (no device down, no exhaustion projected) says so with noValue (None, 0).
  • Queries survive push outputs. With remote_write or otlp, a series receives a sample only when its job runs, and queries look back 5 minutes for the last one (outputs). Gauges are read with last_over_time(metric[window]), the window two to three times the default interval of the job that produces them (15m for a 5-minute job, 2h for an hourly one), and the _info metrics of joins with max by (<id>, <labels>) (last_over_time(..._info[window])). Rates of counters need no window of their own.

items.title: CEL mapping recipes
items.text:
Patterns taken from the built-in templates. The CEL environment and its functions are described in 06-mapping-and-outputs.md.

Enveloped lists. extract.items points to the list inside the envelope (teltonika-rms, aruba-central-classic):

extract:
  items: response.body.data          # {"success": true, "data": [...], "meta": {...}}

Paginate such a list in the simulator with response.itemsField (see 08-simulator.md).

Flattening nested lists. One item per appliance and uplink (meraki-appliance-uplink-statuses):

items: >-
  response.body.map(a, default(a.uplinks, []).map(u, {'serial': a.serial, 'interface': u.interface, 'status': default(u.status, '')})).flatten()

Absent or null fields. default(value, fallback) covers a missing or null field; has() tests a key before reading below it; skipIf drops a sample rather than inventing a value (meraki-dashboard, aruba-central-classic):

labels:
  name: "default(item.name, '')"
  network_id: "has(item.network) ? default(item.network.id, '') : ''"
metrics:
  - name: aruba_ap_clients
    value: toFloat(item.client_count)
    skipIf: "!has(item.client_count) || item.client_count == null"

Timestamps. parseTimestamp reads RFC 3339 by default, or a Go layout; a timestamp metric is a number of seconds (rms-devices):

value: "double(int(parseTimestamp(item.last_connection_at, '2006-01-02 15:04:05')))"

As the timestamp of a sample, it carries the source time of the value (example-sim-devices): timestamp: parseTimestamp(item.updatedAt).

_info metrics. Descriptive attributes go to an _info metric (value 1) that shares an identifier label with the measures, so that queries join them (meraki-devices):

info:
  - name: meraki_device_info
    labels:
      serial: item.serial
      name: "default(item.name, '')"
      model: "default(item.model, '')"

(meraki_device_up == 0) * on (serial) group_left (name, model) meraki_device_info

items.title: Recording real responses
items.text:
tapyr record runs jobs once against the real API, through the budget engine, and writes their responses anonymized:

tapyr record --config ./config --job devices --out ./recording [--anonymize ./anonymize.yaml]
  • Serials, MAC and IP addresses, identifiers, names, emails, phone numbers, coordinates and addresses are replaced by consistent pseudonyms that keep their format (a MAC stays a MAC, an identifier keeps its length and its digits); the same value gets the same pseudonym in every page and in the request variables, so the recording stays consistent.
  • anonymize.yaml adds rules and exceptions:
replace:
  - { path: "data[*].company_name", as: name }   # serial, digits, mac, ipv4, ipv6, email, hostname, name, id, coordinate, address, redact
keep:
  - "data[*].model"
  • report.txt lists every replaced path and rule, never a value. Review the recording before committing anything: free-text fields can still hold identifying data.
  • Only the quota headers of the provider and Retry-After are recorded; request credentials never are.
  • Run it with the configuration and TAPYR_STATE_KEY of tapyr run: it reads the token pair an auth plugin stored (aruba-central-classic), read-only, and never renews a rotating refresh token, which would leave tapyr run with a spent one.

The teltonika-rms fixtures follow the shape of such a recording.

items.title: Linting and contract tests
items.text:
tapyr provider lint providers/teltonika-rms        # one package
tapyr provider lint providers                      # every package of a directory
tapyr provider lint --update providers/my-api      # accept the new samples
tapyr provider lint --catalog providers/my-api     # also require the catalog metadata

The lint loads the package, compiles every template, checks the dashboards (valid JSON, a datasource variable, only metrics of the package or tapyr_ self-metrics), the examples, the required scenarios, then runs the contract test: the jobs of tests/contract.yaml run once against the simulator, on a fake clock starting at 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z, and their samples must equal tests/expected.prom. Every template must be exercised. With --catalog, the catalog metadata of the package and the source of every limit are required too, with existing categories and dates. make lint and the CI lint the built-in packages with --catalog.

items.title: End-to-end tests
items.text:
The packages tested against real platforms have e2e tests in test/e2e/ (build tag e2e), skipped unless their credentials are set:

TAPYR_E2E_MERAKI_API_KEY=... make e2e
TAPYR_E2E_RMS_TOKEN=... make e2e
TAPYR_E2E_RUTOS_URL=https://192.0.2.10 TAPYR_E2E_RUTOS_USERNAME=... TAPYR_E2E_RUTOS_PASSWORD=... make e2e

They run tapyr run for one or two minutes and spend a few requests.

items.title: Auth plugins
items.text: When an auth flow cannot be declared (Aruba Central rotates its refresh tokens), it is written in Go under internal/auth/plugins/<name> and registered in internal/auth/plugins. A plugin validates its auth.plugin.config (secret references as {secret: name}), creates an authenticator per account with a sender of auth requests through the budget engine and a sealed store for its state, and provides its simulator side. See 05-collection.md.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
Start from the symptom. Most answers come from four places, all read-only and without secrets:

Where What it tells tapyr validate --config <paths> --check-secrets Every configuration error, with its file, line and column tapyr plan --config <paths> What every job will spend of every quota, and at which interval it will really run The web UI (/ui/) or the status API (/api/v1/...) Jobs and their last runs with their errors, budgets, the plan, outputs, accounts The logs and /metrics/self Decisions as they happen, and counters over time

Examples below use the default address 127.0.0.1:9790.

items.title: The configuration is rejected
items.text:
tapyr validate and tapyr run print every problem as file:line:column: path: message, and exit with code 2:

config.yaml:8:5: spec.secrets.apiKey: environment variable TAPYR_EXAMPLE_API_KEY is not set
configuration is invalid: 1 error
  • Unknown field, wrong type. Check the field in the configuration reference. Editors catch these as you type with the JSON Schema (see the reference for the yaml-language-server line).
  • Unknown template or provider. tapyr provider list shows the packages Tapyr knows; user packages need settings.providerPaths, and each package README lists its templates.
  • A secret is not set. --check-secrets checks that every referenced environment variable or file exists and is not empty. Without it, validate checks the configuration only, which suits a CI without the secrets.
  • Nothing is collected and no error. configuration is valid: ... 0 accounts, 0 jobs means the paths contain no document: check --config (files must end in .yaml or .yml, hidden files are skipped).

items.title: Tapyr does not start
items.text:
• bind: address already in use: another process listens on the address of settings.server.listen (default 127.0.0.1:9790), often another Tapyr. Stop it or change the address.
  • The state store cannot be opened: the directory of settings.state.path must exist or be creatable, and be writable by the user running Tapyr (uid 65532 in the image).
  • GET /readyz answers 503 with its reasons while something is not ready: the configuration, the state store or an output.

items.title: No data yet
items.text:
• First runs are spread. Jobs start at a random point within the first 10% of their interval (settings.collection.jitter), so that a restart does not fire every request at once: a job polled every hour may wait up to 6 minutes for its first run.
  • Discovery comes first. A fan-out job waits for the first run of its parents (organizations, then networks...). A newly discovered instance runs first within the jitter of its interval, then at its own point of the interval, so that a thousand networks never fire at once: with the default jitter, each level of the chain adds at most a tenth of its interval. After that, the inventory is cached and restarts no longer wait. The Graph page of the UI shows the chain.
  • No output. /metrics serves the samples only with a prometheus output; push outputs deliver to their backend (see their troubleshooting).
  • The job fails. Open it in the UI, or GET /api/v1/jobs/<name>/runs: every run has its result and its error.

items.title: Authentication fails (401, 403)
items.text:
The runs fail with an authentication error, and tapyr_auth_token_requests_total{result="failed"} grows for token-based providers.

  • Check the secret the account refers to: the right variable, no trailing newline in a file, the permissions the provider README asks for (read-only API keys are enough: Tapyr never writes).
  • After a rejected token or login request, Tapyr waits before trying again: 1 minute, then 2, 4... up to 1 hour, so that a wrong password does not lock the account. Fixing the secret and reloading (SIGHUP) ends the wait at once.
  • tapyr_auth_reauth_required at 1 (and the TapyrReauthRequired alert) means the credentials can no longer be renewed on their own, for example an expired Aruba Central refresh token: create new ones, update the secret and reload. The provider README explains how.

items.title: Quota problems
items.text:
The budget engine is meant to make these impossible: when they happen, one of its inputs is wrong. The Budgets page of the UI and GET /api/v1/budgets show every limit and scope: what Tapyr used, what is left as Tapyr counts it and as the provider reports it, the external usage and the projection.

Symptom Likely cause What to do tapyr_budget_unexpected_429_total grows The provider enforces a limit the definition does not declare, declares too high, or scopes differently (per IP, per organization) Tapyr backs off on its own; report it on the provider package with the endpoint and the response headers (the debug endpoint shows them, redacted) tapyr_budget_external_usage high, the quota runs out early Another client uses the same quota: the vendor UI, a script, another integration Give Tapyr its own credentials, or a budget.share tapyr_budget_limit_mismatch at 1 The provider announces another maximum than the definition (another plan, another account size) Tapyr follows the headers; the definition should use max: auto Consumption above the plan More fan-out instances or pages than estimated, many retries Compare tapyr plan with the runs (requests, pages, retries per run) Jobs run slower than their interval The quota is too small for the desired intervals: the planner stretched them See below tapyr plan exits with code 3, TapyrPlanInfeasible critical jobs alone exceed a quota Raise their intervals, lower some to high, reduce the fan-out Requests refused with quota_exhausted right after a restart The state store was lost (no volume): Tapyr restarted from 0 while the provider still counted Keep the state store on persistent storage (Operations)

items.title: Jobs run less often than configured
items.text:
The planner gives every job an effective interval that fits the quotas, and stretches the lower priorities first (Concepts). It is working as intended; to see why, read the plan: tapyr plan, the Plan page of the UI, or GET /api/v1/plan. Each stretched job says by how much, why, and which quota constrains it:
