job network-devices  desired 5m  effective 1h  24 runs x 1 page = 25  (stretched x12.00, priority normal, quota example-sim/daily account=demo)

To change the outcome: raise the priority of what matters (and lower the rest), raise intervals of jobs that can wait, filter the fan-out (forEach.filter), or get a larger quota. The log line effective interval changed records every change with its reason.

Runs can also start late without any stretch when they wait for rate or concurrency limits (TapyrJobLagging): tapyr_budget_wait_seconds shows the waits by limit.

items.title: Metrics are wrong or missing
items.text:
• Mapping errors. tapyr_mapping_errors_total{job, metric} counts the samples a mapping could not produce, for example a field the API no longer sends. Enable the debug endpoint (settings.server.debug.enabled: true) and open the Live debug page: the last raw response of the job, side by side with the samples it produced.
  • Series disappear. A series absent from the last successful run goes stale at once (a device removed from the API). After failed runs, the series stay until staleAfter, 3 times the effective interval by default, then go stale too.
  • Labels collide. A label set by the mapping and by the account, target or job takes the value of the job, then target, then account. settings.mapping.labelConflict: error turns collisions into run errors instead.
  • The self-metrics have exported_job instead of job. The scrape of /metrics/self needs honor_labels: true (Operations).

items.title: Samples do not reach the backend
items.text:
GET /api/v1/outputs and the Outputs page show the queue and the last results of every push output.

  • tapyr_output_send_failures_total{class="rejected"} with 401 or 403: the credentials of the output.
  • class="out_of_order": the backend refuses samples older than the ones it has. Prometheus needs out-of-order ingestion for source timestamps (Outputs); otherwise another writer sends the same series.
  • tapyr_output_samples_dropped_total{reason="queue_full"}: the backend is slower than the collection, or was down longer than the queue lasts (Sizing the queue).

items.title: A reload changed nothing
items.text:
• configuration reload rejected: the running configuration is kept in the logs, and tapyr_config_last_reload_success at 0: the new configuration is invalid; tapyr validate shows why.
  • settings changed that take effect after a restart: server, state.path and log need a restart.

items.title: Asking for help
items.text:
Open an issue with:

  • tapyr version, and how Tapyr runs (binary, image, Kubernetes);
  • the configuration, secrets removed, and the provider package involved;
  • the relevant log lines, tapyr plan output and status API responses. Tapyr redacts secrets from all of them, but read them before pasting: they show your inventory;
  • best of all, a reproduction against the simulator (tapyr sim --provider <name> --scenario <scenario>), or real responses recorded with tapyr record, which anonymizes them.

Report vulnerabilities privately, as explained in the security policy, never in a public issue.

items.title: ADR 0001 - Go as implementation language
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02

items.title: Context
items.text: Tapyr is a long-running collector with fine-grained concurrency (rate limits, concurrency limits, many simultaneous job runs), persistent state, and standard observability outputs. It should be trivial to deploy.

items.title: Decision
items.text: Implement Tapyr in Go, distributed as a single static binary (no CGO) and a Docker image.

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• Python: faster to prototype, rich vendor SDKs, but weaker concurrency ergonomics for this kind of scheduler, heavier deployment, and vendor SDKs would push towards vendor-specific code.
  • Rust: excellent performance and safety, but a smaller observability ecosystem for our needs and a higher contribution barrier.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Native access to the Prometheus and OpenTelemetry Go ecosystems and to cel-go.
  • Same language as most exporters and as Grafana Alloy / OTel Collector, familiar to contributors in the observability space.
  • No CGO constraint: pure-Go SQLite (modernc.org/sqlite).

items.title: ADR 0002 - CEL as the mapping and expression language
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
path: ADR 0002 - CEL as the mapping and expression language

items.title: Context
items.text: Provider packages must transform arbitrary JSON responses into metrics, compute pagination conditions, extract tokens, and filter discovery items. Provider packages are meant to be written by the community and executed by every Tapyr user, so the language must be safe, predictable and checkable before runtime.
path: ADR 0002 - CEL as the mapping and expression language

items.title: Decision
items.text: Use CEL (Common Expression Language, github.com/google/cel-go) for every runtime expression, wrapped in a declarative structure (items, metrics, labels, value...) so most mappings stay trivial.
path: ADR 0002 - CEL as the mapping and expression language

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text: Option Why not jq (gojq) Powerful and well known, but untyped, termination not guaranteed, harder to bound in cost; risky for community packages JSONPath (RFC 9535) Standardized, but selection only, no computation JMESPath Selection-oriented, limited computation, less active ecosystem OTTL Designed to transform existing OpenTelemetry data inside the Collector, not arbitrary JSON expr-lang Pleasant, but library-specific rather than a specification Lua / JavaScript Turing-complete, sandboxing burden, too much power for mappings
path: ADR 0002 - CEL as the mapping and expression language

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Non Turing-complete: expressions always terminate; cost can be estimated and capped.
  • Type-checked at compile time: tapyr validate catches errors before deployment.
  • Proven in Kubernetes (validation rules, admission policies), Envoy and Google IAM: a known, specified language with a future.
  • Extensible with custom functions (timestamps, sizes, durations, MAC normalization).
  • Slightly less familiar to network engineers than jq: documentation must include a mapping cookbook.
path: ADR 0002 - CEL as the mapping and expression language

items.title: ADR 0003 - YAML configuration with a Kubernetes-like envelope and generated JSON Schemas
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
path: ADR 0003 - YAML configuration with a Kubernetes-like envelope and generated JSON Schemas

items.title: Context
items.text: Configuration must be declarative, Git-friendly, splittable across files, validated precisely, and pleasant to edit with autocompletion. Provider packages and user configuration share the same format.
path: ADR 0003 - YAML configuration with a Kubernetes-like envelope and generated JSON Schemas

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• YAML, multi-document, with apiVersion / kind / metadata / spec.
  • apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1, bumped on breaking changes.
  • Go types are the source of truth; JSON Schemas are generated from them and committed in schemas/.
  • Documents can live in any number of files and directories; references are by name.
path: ADR 0003 - YAML configuration with a Kubernetes-like envelope and generated JSON Schemas

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• HCL or Alloy syntax: expressive, but less universal tooling and a steeper learning curve for users.
  • TOML (Telegraf style): awkward for deeply nested structures such as mappings.
  • Single monolithic file: does not scale to many providers and accounts.
path: ADR 0003 - YAML configuration with a Kubernetes-like envelope and generated JSON Schemas

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Editors (VS Code YAML extension) get validation and autocompletion through the schemas.
  • The documentation reference can be generated from the schemas.
  • Versioned format from day one, a prerequisite for a community provider ecosystem.
path: ADR 0003 - YAML configuration with a Kubernetes-like envelope and generated JSON Schemas

items.title: ADR 0004 - Declarative provider packages shared by collector and simulator
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
path: ADR 0004 - Declarative provider packages shared by collector and simulator

items.title: Context
items.text: Supporting a new API should not require Go code, and providers must be testable without vendor access. Rate limits declared in one place must drive both the collector (to respect them) and the simulator (to enforce them).
path: ADR 0004 - Declarative provider packages shared by collector and simulator

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• Vendor knowledge lives in provider packages: provider.yaml (auth, limits, pagination, errors), job templates, simulator definition and fixtures, dashboards, contract tests, README.
  • The simulator reads the same Provider document and reuses the budget package server-side to enforce limits.
  • Go code is limited to generic mechanisms and auth plugins for flows that cannot be expressed declaratively.
  • Packages are versioned (semver); built-in packages are embedded in the binary.
path: ADR 0004 - Declarative provider packages shared by collector and simulator

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• Go plugins per vendor (Terraform-style): maximum flexibility, but high contribution barrier and compiled distribution.
  • Separate mock servers (e.g. generic mocking tools): limits would be declared twice and drift.
path: ADR 0004 - Declarative provider packages shared by collector and simulator

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Community contributions are accessible to engineers who know an API but not Go.
  • A provider package is self-contained and testable in CI with no network.
  • The declarative model must be rich enough; when it is not, we extend the generic mechanisms rather than adding vendor code.
  • Opens the door to OCI distribution and a registry later.
path: ADR 0004 - Declarative provider packages shared by collector and simulator

items.title: ADR 0005 - Embedded SQLite for persistent state
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
path: ADR 0005 - Embedded SQLite for persistent state

items.title: Context
items.text: Daily and monthly quotas must survive restarts, rotating refresh tokens must never be lost, inventory caches avoid wasting quota, and the series registry drives staleness across restarts. The MVP is single-instance and must not require a database server.
path: ADR 0005 - Embedded SQLite for persistent state

items.title: Decision
items.text: Use embedded SQLite through modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go), behind a state.Store interface. Default path ./data/tapyr.db. Batched writes, flush every few seconds and on shutdown. Tokens encrypted at rest when TAPYR_STATE_KEY is set.
path: ADR 0005 - Embedded SQLite for persistent state

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• bbolt / badger: key-value only; SQLite makes run history and timelines easier to query.
  • Plain JSON files: fragile under crashes and concurrency.
  • Redis: requires a server; kept as a possible backend for the future distributed mode.
path: ADR 0005 - Embedded SQLite for persistent state

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Single static binary preserved.
  • The state.Store interface keeps a future shared backend possible.
  • A volume is required in containers for persistence (documented).
path: ADR 0005 - Embedded SQLite for persistent state

items.title: ADR 0006 - Read-only web UI embedded in the binary
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
path: ADR 0006 - Read-only web UI embedded in the binary

items.title: Context
items.text: Users need to see what Tapyr is doing (providers, jobs, budgets, plan, errors) quickly, in the spirit of the Grafana Alloy UI. Configuration must stay declarative and versioned in Git.
path: ADR 0006 - Read-only web UI embedded in the binary

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• A read-only web UI in the MVP, built with React + Vite + TypeScript, compiled and embedded with go:embed.
  • The UI consumes only the public read-only status API (/api/v1) and SSE events.
  • No editing capability in the UI.
path: ADR 0006 - Read-only web UI embedded in the binary

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• No UI (Grafana only): Grafana covers metrics, but not effective configuration, plan, fan-out instances or live mapping debug.
  • Server-rendered UI (Go templates + htmx): lighter build chain, but the UI will grow (graph, timelines, future mapping assistant and impact simulation) and benefits from a component ecosystem (@xyflow/react).
  • Editable UI: conflicts with configuration-as-code and multiplies complexity.
path: ADR 0006 - Read-only web UI embedded in the binary

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• The status API is designed first and stays the single contract, which keeps other clients possible.
  • The build requires Node in CI; end users still get one binary.
  • Security: the UI shows infrastructure details; default listen on localhost, optional basic auth.
path: ADR 0006 - Read-only web UI embedded in the binary

items.title: ADR 0007 - Apache License 2.0
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02

items.title: Context
items.text: Tapyr aims at broad adoption, including in companies, and at a community of provider contributors.

items.title: Decision
items.text: License the project under Apache License 2.0.

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• MIT: similar permissiveness, but no explicit patent grant.
  • AGPL: protects against closed SaaS reuse but discourages corporate adoption and contributions.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Same license as Prometheus and OpenTelemetry, familiar to the target audience.
  • Explicit patent grant reassures companies.
  • Contributions are accepted under the same license (DCO sign-off recommended in CONTRIBUTING).

items.title: Notes
items.text: • 2026-11-04: DCO sign-off is not required. The inbound=outbound terms of CONTRIBUTING.md apply: contributions are licensed under the Apache License 2.0, like the project.

items.title: ADR 0008 - Build OTLP payloads directly, not through the OpenTelemetry metrics SDK
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
path: ADR 0008 - Build OTLP payloads directly, not through the OpenTelemetry metrics SDK

items.title: Context
items.text: Collected samples often carry source timestamps from the vendor API, may arrive late or out of order, and must sometimes be marked stale. The OpenTelemetry metrics SDK is designed for instrumenting applications: it aggregates measurements and assigns timestamps at collection time.
path: ADR 0008 - Build OTLP payloads directly, not through the OpenTelemetry metrics SDK

items.title: Decision
items.text: Build OTLP metric payloads directly with go.opentelemetry.io/collector/pdata (pmetric) and send them with OTLP/HTTP or OTLP/gRPC clients. The OpenTelemetry SDK may still be used for Tapyr's own telemetry if needed.
path: ADR 0008 - Build OTLP payloads directly, not through the OpenTelemetry metrics SDK

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text: • OpenTelemetry metrics SDK for collected data: cannot carry source timestamps, aggregates values, no staleness flag control.
path: ADR 0008 - Build OTLP payloads directly, not through the OpenTelemetry metrics SDK

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Full control over timestamps, start times of cumulative sums, and FLAG_NO_RECORDED_VALUE for staleness.
  • We own batching, retries and partial-success handling for the OTLP output.
path: ADR 0008 - Build OTLP payloads directly, not through the OpenTelemetry metrics SDK

items.title: ADR 0009 - Window values exposed as gauges by default
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
path: ADR 0009 - Window values exposed as gauges by default

items.title: Context
items.text: Many vendor APIs return values aggregated over a time window ("bytes over the last 5 minutes", "average over the last hour") instead of cumulative counters.
path: ADR 0009 - Window values exposed as gauges by default

items.title: Decision
items.text: Expose window values as gauges by default, with names stating the window (..._5m). Offer optional counter reconstruction (type: counter, accumulate: true) that sums non-overlapping windows into a persisted monotonic counter.
path: ADR 0009 - Window values exposed as gauges by default

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• Always reconstruct counters: elegant for PromQL rate(), but fragile with overlapping or irregular windows and misleading after gaps.
  • Expose raw without naming conventions: ambiguous for users.
path: ADR 0009 - Window values exposed as gauges by default

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Honest default semantics; users query gauges directly.
  • Reconstruction available where windows are reliable.
  • Provider package reviews must check window naming.
path: ADR 0009 - Window values exposed as gauges by default

items.title: ADR 0010 - Documentation site built from this repository
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-05
path: ADR 0010 - Documentation site built from this repository

items.title: Context
items.text:
The documentation is Markdown in this repository (docs/, the provider and example READMEs) and is read on GitHub. A documentation site is easier to read, search and link, and lets a user read the documentation of the version they run. The static documentation website was out of scope of v0.1.0 (01-vision-and-scope.md); issue #7 is the agreement it asks for.

The documentation describes behavior: a pull request that changes behavior updates the spec, the examples or the provider README in the same commit (definition of done in AGENTS.md). Whatever we build must keep that.
path: ADR 0010 - Documentation site built from this repository

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• Content stays in this repository. Every page is written here, reviewed with the code it describes, and frozen by each release tag. Pages keep working on GitHub: links are relative, between files of the repository.
  • The site is built in a dedicated repository. It holds the engine (Zensical, by the Material for MkDocs team): configuration, theme, home page, build and deployment to docs.tapyr.eu. It never edits the content: a fix to a page is a pull request here.
  • The manifest docs/site.yml lists the published pages and their order. A page added here appears on the site without a change in the site repository. Every Markdown file of the source directories it names is either published or listed as unpublished, so a new page cannot be forgotten.
  • The contract is a tool of this repository, internal/tools/docsite:
  • check validates the manifest and every relative link of the Markdown files of the repository, anchors included (part of make lint);
  • export -ref <tag> -out <dir> -index <file> writes the pages at their site paths, with links rewritten: to the site page when the target is published, to the file on GitHub at that ref otherwise; images are copied. The index file holds the navigation, in the nav format of mkdocs.yml, and the source file of every page for the "edit this page" links.

The site repository checks out a tag of this repository and runs its export. Site paths drop the docs/ prefix, and a README.md becomes the index.md of its directory (providers/meraki-dashboard/README.md is /providers/meraki-dashboard/). - Anchors are GitHub heading slugs (lowercase, punctuation removed, spaces as hyphens); the site configures its slug function to produce the same ones (pymdownx.slugs.slugify with case: lower; an export of every page built with Zensical 0.0.74 resolved all its internal links and anchors). - Versions. One documentation version per minor release, built from the latest tag of that minor (/0.1/ from v0.1.2, then v0.1.3), /latest/ for the latest stable minor, /dev/ for main. Release candidates are not published. Older minors stay online with an outdated banner; the version selector lists the last three and dev. The first published version is 0.1, from v0.1.1, the first tag with the manifest. - Reference pages are generated, from the JSON Schemas for the configuration, and are never written by hand.
path: ADR 0010 - Documentation site built from this repository

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• Site and content in this repository. One repository, one pull request; but the Python tool chain of the site, its theme work and its deployment rights would live in the Go repository and its CI. The manifest and docsite keep the boundary small enough that a second repository costs little.
  • Content moved to the site repository. Documentation changes would need a second pull request, reviewed apart from the code, and would drift from the releases (the Kubernetes website model).
  • Site from GitHub Markdown as is (no manifest, no export). Links that leave docs/ (provider and example READMEs, configuration files) break on the site, and the navigation lives in the site repository, out of sight of the pull requests that add pages.
  • MkDocs with Material for MkDocs. In maintenance mode, its authors moved to Zensical, which reads the same configuration.
path: ADR 0010 - Documentation site built from this repository

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Writing documentation does not change: Markdown here, relative links, make lint catches a broken link or anchor before the site does.
  • A new Markdown file in docs/ must be added to docs/site.yml, in nav or in unpublished.
  • The output of docsite export (paths, link rewriting, index file) is an interface: changing it means a coordinated change of the site repository. So is the output of tapyr provider list --output json, from which the site builds the provider catalog (ADR 0011, versioned by its schemaVersion).
  • Zensical is young (0.0.x) and its native versioning is on its roadmap; the site repository pins its version and uses the mike fork it documents meanwhile.
  • v0.1.0 has no documentation version on the site.
path: ADR 0010 - Documentation site built from this repository

items.title: ADR 0011 - Generic engine, network-first launch and a provider catalog
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-06
path: ADR 0011 - Generic engine, network-first launch and a provider catalog

items.title: Context
items.text:
v0.1 ships four provider packages, all for network equipment: Aruba Central (classic), Cisco Meraki, Teltonika RMS and Teltonika RutOS. The problem Tapyr solves, collecting metrics from APIs whose quota is scarce, is not specific to networks: a survey of candidate APIs (provider ideas) found it in security services, Internet measurement, cloud costs, developer platforms, energy and sport. Most of them fit the configuration model as it is; some need mechanisms the budget engine does not have yet.

At the same time, an open source project that claims to do everything struggles to find its first users, and the provider ecosystems that work (Terraform Registry, Ansible Galaxy, Grafana dashboards) show that discoverability and trust signals decide whether contributions keep coming. Today a provider package carries a name, a version, a description and a documentation link: nothing tells who maintains it or how it was tested, except the prose of its README. Users can already load their own packages from settings.providerPaths; the built-in packages are the ones in providers/, embedded in the binary.
path: ADR 0011 - Generic engine, network-first launch and a provider catalog

items.title: Decision
items.text:
1. Generic engine. The core makes no network-specific assumption: any metric-oriented API must be expressible as a provider package. A provider that needs a missing mechanism gets a generic, configurable one, never vendor logic in internal/ (the design principles of AGENTS.md).
  2. Network-first launch. Networks are the first use case, not the boundary. The README, the site and the specs lead with network equipment, where the built-in packages are; other domains come with the engine features they need, ideally from contributions.
  3. Catalog metadata on provider packages, in v0.2.0. Two independent axes describe a package instead of a single trust level:
  4. tier: who maintains it. official packages are maintained by the Tapyr maintainers; community packages by their contributors, named in maintainers;
  5. validation: how it was tested. status is simulator or real-platform, with the date and the platformVersion of the last validation.

With displayName, categories (a controlled vocabulary kept in the repository) and maintainers, and a structured source on every limit (kind: vendor-docs, measured or assumed, with a url and a date). The fields are optional in the schema, so that user packages keep working; tapyr provider lint --catalog requires them, and the CI of this repository runs it on the built-in packages. 4. One repository for official and community packages. A community package is contributed by pull request to providers/, passes the same CI as the official ones (lint, contract test, simulator) and is embedded in the binary. Its tier and maintainers say who answers for it, and the catalog shows them. A community package that is broken and whose maintainers no longer answer may be removed in a minor release, announced in the changelog; users who still need it load the last version from providerPaths. 5. A phased ecosystem. - Phase 1, from v0.2: a static provider catalog on tapyr.eu, built by the site repository from tapyr provider list --output json, as the documentation site is built from this repository (ADR 0010). Each entry links the page of its package on docs.tapyr.eu. - Phase 2, later and only if justified by packages maintained outside this repository: provider packages distributed as OCI artifacts, evaluating Artifact Hub before building a registry. It stays out of scope until an issue and an agreement (01-vision-and-scope.md).
path: ADR 0011 - Generic engine, network-first launch and a provider catalog

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• Network-only scope. Simpler to explain, but it limits a generic engine and the community that could grow around it for no technical reason.
  • Three trust tiers (official in the main repository, verified tested on a real platform, community passing CI only). They mix who maintains a package with how it was tested: meraki-dashboard is official but validated on its simulator only, the Teltonika packages are official and validated on real platforms. Two axes keep both facts.
  • Community packages outside the binary (a providers/community/ directory, or a separate repository, loaded through providerPaths). The binary would not ship packages its maintainers do not answer for, but users would download a directory and track its versions by hand, which phase 2 solves properly. Revisited with phase 2.
  • An open catalog from day one (Galaxy style, anyone publishes). Packages of uneven quality, abandoned ones, and no trust signal yet to tell them apart.
  • A registry with accounts and uploads now. A high cost with no value before there are packages to distribute.
path: ADR 0011 - Generic engine, network-first launch and a provider catalog

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Writing a package takes a little more work (metadata, structured sources of limits), and building the catalog much less: it is generated, never written by hand.
  • The engine is generic in principle but not yet in features. The survey found five mechanisms that other domains need: a cost per request, quota windows aligned on any duration, quota sync from expressions, windows starting at the first request, rate limiting signaled other than by a status (engine gaps). Each one is designed in its own issue, with a spec change and an ADR when it changes the reservation algorithm or the ledger.
  • The binary grows with every community package, and the maintainers review packages for APIs they cannot test: the review rests on the simulator, the contract test and the cited sources, and the catalog says what was validated.
  • A metric naming convention per domain will be needed when the second domain lands (today <prefix>_<object>_<measure>_<unit>, docs/providers.md); it is decided then, with the first package of that domain.
  • The output of tapyr provider list --output json becomes an interface of the site repository, versioned like the output of docsite export.
path: ADR 0011 - Generic engine, network-first launch and a provider catalog

items.title: ADR 0012 - Processing per output, first step: keep and drop metrics and labels
items.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-10
path: ADR 0012 - Processing per output, first step: keep and drop metrics and labels

items.title: Context
items.text:
Every series Tapyr sends has a cost downstream. Hosted backends bill by active series and data points per minute; self-hosted ones pay in memory, disk and query time. Today every output receives every metric of the jobs routed to it, and the only way to send less is to change the mappings of a provider package, which changes every output at once and forks the package.

Users ask for what every collection pipeline offers (Prometheus, the OpenTelemetry Collector, Alloy, vmagent): keep or drop metrics and labels per destination, then aggregate, send less often to an expensive backend, and see what each choice costs. Tapyr also knows where every metric comes from, since it makes the API call: when no output consumes the metrics of a job, the call itself could be skipped, saving API quota as well as ingestion.

This ADR decides the first step only: filtering metrics and labels per output. The other parts are follow-up issues (see Consequences), each to be designed with its own constraints (counters, staleness, source timestamps).
path: ADR 0012 - Processing per output, first step: keep and drop metrics and labels

items.title: Decision
items.text:
1. Rules per output. An Output gains spec.processing, an ordered list of rules applied to the samples of the jobs sent to that output only. The semantics are those of Prometheus metric_relabel_configs, with camelCase field names, so that rules written for Prometheus carry over:
spec:
  type: remote_write
  processing:
    - action: drop
      sourceLabels: [__name__]
      regex: "meraki_uplink_.*"
    - action: labeldrop
      regex: firmware
Action Fields Effect keep sourceLabels (required), separator (default ;), regex (default (.*)) keeps the samples whose joined source label values match drop same drops the samples whose joined source label values match labelkeep regex (required) keeps only the labels whose name matches labeldrop regex (required) removes the labels whose name matches

regex is RE2, fully anchored (^(?:regex)$). __name__ is the metric name; a missing label is the empty string. Rules apply in order, a dropped sample stops at once.

  1. Where it applies. On the delivery of each output, after the mapping and the counter reconstruction, before deduplication, and before the externalLabels that the output adds when it sends. The series registry stays shared: outputs without rules cost nothing more. Without rules, nothing changes.

  2. Staleness and deduplication follow the series an output receives.

  3. For an output with rules, the registry keeps, per job instance, the set of processed series last sent to it. A series in the previous set and absent from the current one goes stale for that output: a stale marker for push outputs, removal from the exposition for the pull output. This covers a series that a rule starts dropping after a reload (marked stale once at the next run of its instance) and a label that labeldrop removes (the old series goes stale, the new one appears).
  4. After a restart, the previous set of an instance is derived from the raw series of the snapshot with the current rules: nothing new is persisted.
  5. Deduplication uses the processed series key.

  6. Two samples of one run that end up with the same series (a labeldrop removing the label that told them apart) are a configuration problem: the first is kept, the others are dropped and counted in tapyr_output_samples_dropped_total{reason="duplicate"}, which the TapyrOutputDropping alert reports.

  7. The pull output (prometheus) is processed like the others: it exposes the processed samples of the last successful run of every instance.

  8. Not processed: Tapyr's self-metrics, on /metrics/self or pushed through an output (selfMetrics.outputs): they are the view on Tapyr itself, and filtering them could hide a problem.

  9. Validation (tapyr validate, at load):

  10. errors: an unknown action, a missing required field, a field an action does not take, an invalid regular expression or label name, a labelkeep whose regex does not match __name__, a labeldrop whose regex matches __name__; the fields of later actions (targetLabel, replacement) are unknown fields;

  11. warnings: a keep or drop on __name__ alone that matches no metric declared by the templates of the jobs sent to the output.

  12. Visibility: tapyr_output_samples_filtered_total{output} counts the samples removed by keep and drop. It is a separate counter because filtering is intended, while tapyr_output_samples_dropped_total and its alert are about losses.
path: ADR 0012 - Processing per output, first step: keep and drop metrics and labels

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.text:
• Leave it to a pipeline downstream (OpenTelemetry Collector, Alloy, vmagent). It works today and stays possible, but it is one more component to run and it filters data already collected.
  • The full relabeling set at once (replace, labelmap, hashmod). Renaming __name__ changes the metadata (type, help, unit) and the OTLP metric names, and can create type conflicts between metrics that validation checks today; it deserves its own design.
  • CEL conditions (when). One language everywhere, but simple keep and drop rules become verbose and do not carry over from Prometheus; kept for later, for what relabeling cannot express.
  • OTTL. Standard in the OpenTelemetry Collector, but tied to its data model and unknown to Prometheus users.
  • Rules per job instead of per output. Simpler, but one output could not get more detail than another, which is the main use case (a complete local backend, a reduced hosted one).
  • Stale markers computed with the current rules only (no per-output sets). No memory cost, but a series dropped by a new rule, or renamed by a new labeldrop, would stop without a stale marker and linger in the backend for its lookback.
path: ADR 0012 - Processing per output, first step: keep and drop metrics and labels

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Users reduce what an output receives without forking a provider package; a local backend can stay complete next to a reduced hosted one.
  • The registry costs memory proportional to the series of the outputs with rules (one more set per instance and output).
  • A rule change applies at the next successful run of each instance, not at the reload.
  • labeldrop can merge series; the duplicates it creates are dropped and counted, not silently overwritten.
  • Follow-up issues, out of this step: skipping the API calls whose metrics no output consumes (#56), cost visibility with series estimates in tapyr plan and a series limit per output (#57), aggregation before sending (#58), an interval per output (#59), sending a series only when its value changes (#60). replace, labelmap and CEL conditions come with the first of them that needs them.
path: ADR 0012 - Processing per output, first step: keep and drop metrics and labels

items.title: Helm chart
items.text: Tapyr on Kubernetes with Helm: one replica, non-root, a read-only root file system, probes on /readyz and /healthz, the state store on a volume, and the configuration as a ConfigMap whose changes roll the pod out.

items.title: Install
items.text:
1. Write your values: the accounts, jobs and output in config (the README of each provider package has an example).
existingSecret: tapyr
config: |
  apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
  kind: Account
  metadata: { name: campus }
  spec:
    provider: meraki-dashboard
    secrets: { apiKey: { env: TAPYR_MERAKI_API_KEY } }
  ---
  apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
  kind: Job
  metadata: { name: device-availabilities }
  spec: { account: campus, template: meraki-device-availabilities }
  ---
  apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
  kind: Output
  metadata: { name: prom }
  spec: { type: prometheus }
  1. Create the Secret with the environment variables the configuration refers to ({ env: NAME }) and TAPYR_STATE_KEY, which encrypts the tokens kept in the state store. From a file of NAME=value lines, kept out of Git:
kubectl create namespace tapyr
kubectl -n tapyr create secret generic tapyr --from-env-file=tapyr.env
  1. Install, pinned to a version with --version:
helm install tapyr oci://ghcr.io/kentrow/charts/tapyr --namespace tapyr --values my-values.yaml
kubectl -n tapyr port-forward svc/tapyr 9790:9790    # then http://127.0.0.1:9790/ui/

The chart is signed: Install shows how to verify it. Its version is the version of Tapyr.

items.title: Values
items.text:
Value Default What it is config empty Your Account, Job and Output documents, as YAML separated by ---. No Settings document: see settings settings {} Merged into the spec of the Settings document, which the chart writes. server.listen and state.path are set by the chart existingSecret empty A Secret whose keys become environment variables. The chart never holds a secret: values end up in Git and in the Helm history image.repository, .tag, .pullPolicy ghcr.io/kentrow/tapyr, the version of the chart, IfNotPresent The image imagePullSecrets [] For a private registry persistence.enabled, .size, .storageClass, .existingClaim true, 1Gi, empty, empty The volume of the state store service.type, .port, .annotations ClusterIP, 9790, {} /metrics, /metrics/self, the UI and the status API ingress.enabled, .className, .annotations, .host, .tls, .paths off, empty, {}, empty, [], /, /ui and /api See Ingress serviceMonitor.enabled, .labels, .interval off, {}, empty A ServiceMonitor of the Prometheus Operator, for the samples and the self-metrics resources requests 50m, 64Mi, limit 256Mi About 75 MiB of memory for 22,000 series: adjust to your inventories podSecurityContext, securityContext non-root, uid 65532, read-only root, no capability Security contexts terminationGracePeriodSeconds 30 Shutdown flushes the state store and the outputs extraEnv, extraVolumes, extraVolumeMounts [] For secret files ({ file: /path }) and provider packages of your own (settings.providerPaths) podLabels, podAnnotations, nodeSelector, tolerations, affinity empty Scheduling and metadata of the pod

Unknown values are refused. There is no replica count on purpose: a second instance would spend the same quotas without coordinating. The Recreate strategy stops the old pod before the new one opens the state store.

items.title: Ingress
items.text:
The web UI and the status API are read-only, but they show your accounts, jobs, endpoints, quotas and errors, and the raw responses of the APIs when the live debug is on. They have no authentication by default: when you enable the Ingress, authenticate at the Ingress controller, or with Tapyr itself, the credentials coming from existingSecret:

ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  host: tapyr.example.com
settings:
  server:
    basicAuth:
      username: { env: TAPYR_UI_USER }
      password: { env: TAPYR_UI_PASSWORD }

The default paths are the UI and the status API only: /metrics and /metrics/self stay inside the cluster, for Prometheus to scrape through the Service. The UI is served at the root of the host, not under a sub-path.

items.title: Operate
items.text:
• Configuration changes. Change the values and run helm upgrade: the pod restarts with the new configuration, and the state store keeps what was already spent.
  • State. Keep the volume: it remembers what was already spent of the daily and monthly quotas, and the rotated tokens. helm uninstall deletes the volume the chart created.
  • Logs. kubectl -n tapyr logs deploy/tapyr, in JSON.

items.title: Demo compose
items.text:
This compose runs Tapyr against the simulators of the built-in providers, without any vendor account. Its services:

Service What it does Address sim tapyr sim --all: one simulator per built-in provider, with its auth, pagination and limits (429 with Retry-After and quota headers) inside the compose network only tapyr collects from the simulators (tapyr/config.yaml) and pushes the samples to VictoriaMetrics by remote write http://127.0.0.1:9790/ui/ victoriametrics stores the samples and scrapes the self-metrics of Tapyr on /metrics/self http://127.0.0.1:8428/vmui/ grafana the Tapyr / Overview dashboard and the dashboard of every provider, anonymous read access http://127.0.0.1:3000 
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f tapyr     # JSON logs
docker compose down -v           # stop and forget the data

The first samples arrive within a minute (the demo spreads the first runs over 1% of their interval instead of the default 10%). The ports listen on 127.0.0.1 only.

The simulators listen at 8081 plus the portOffset of their package (sim/sim.yaml): aruba-central-classic 8081, example-sim 8082, meraki-dashboard 8083, teltonika-rms 8084, teltonika-rutos 8085. The credentials in compose.yaml are the ones the simulators accept; none of them is a real secret.

items.title: Try the fault scenarios
items.text:
Every provider package has a quota-tight scenario (a quota smaller than the plan expects, or another client consuming it) and a bad-day scenario (errors, latency, an outage). Start the simulators with one of them and watch Tapyr adapt in the Budgets and Plan pages of the UI and in the Quotas row of the overview dashboard:

SIM_SCENARIO=quota-tight docker compose up -d sim
SIM_SCENARIO=bad-day docker compose up -d sim
docker compose up -d sim           # back to the default behavior

A scenario is a timeline that starts with the simulators. quota-tight acts at once. bad-day waits an hour before its first fault, then goes through added latency, errors on the main routes and a short outage, at times of their own in every package (sim/scenarios/bad-day.yaml): the outage of RutOS after 1 hour, the errors after 2 hours, the outages of Meraki and RMS after 4 hours. To see it sooner, run the simulators faster than real time:

SIM_SCENARIO=bad-day SIM_TIME_SCALE=10 docker compose up -d sim

The scenarios then play ten times faster: the outage of RutOS after 6 minutes, the errors after 12, the other outages after 24. The faults get shorter as well, and the quota windows of the simulators run faster too: well above 10, most faults end before the jobs of the demo run again, and Tapyr hardly sees them. Retries absorb most of the errors: look for them on the Retries per minute, by reason panel of the Tapyr / Overview dashboard rather than in the logs.

items.title: With your own build
items.text:
The compose uses the image of the release. To try a local build:

make docker                                   # from the root of the repository: tapyr:dev
TAPYR_IMAGE=tapyr:dev docker compose up -d

items.title: Example configuration
items.text:
A small configuration for the built-in example-sim provider (providers/example-sim/), used by make run and by the CLI tests.

Run it against the built-in simulator, in two terminals:

go run ./cmd/tapyr sim --provider example-sim
TAPYR_EXAMPLE_API_KEY=sim-api-key go run ./cmd/tapyr run --config ./examples/config
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9790/metrics

go run ./cmd/tapyr validate --config ./examples/config --check-secrets reports the API key when TAPYR_EXAMPLE_API_KEY is not set.

demo-network-devices discovers its instances: the sites (demo-sites) list the networks of each site (demo.example-sim-networks, run implicitly), and every network gets its own instance. tapyr plan needs the expected number of instances of a fan-out before the first runs:

TAPYR_EXAMPLE_API_KEY=sim-api-key go run ./cmd/tapyr plan --config ./examples/config \
  --fanout example-sim-sites=3 --fanout example-sim-networks=5

Send SIGHUP to tapyr run after editing the file to reload it without a restart.

While it runs, Tapyr describes itself:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9790/metrics/self | grep '^tapyr_budget'   # quotas, used and remaining
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9790/api/v1/jobs                            # jobs, intervals, last runs
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9790/api/v1/budgets                         # every limit and scope
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9790/readyz

The status API is described in /api/v1/openapi.yaml. To push the samples to VictoriaMetrics or an OpenTelemetry Collector instead of (or as well as) serving /metrics, add a remote_write or otlp output: see docs/outputs.md.

items.title: Kubernetes
items.text:
With Helm, use the chart. Otherwise, plain manifests, applied with Kustomize (kubectl apply -k): a Deployment of one replica, its Service, a volume for the state store and the configuration as a ConfigMap.

File What it is kustomization.yaml Namespace tapyr, image tag, the ConfigMap generated from config.yaml config.yaml The configuration of Tapyr, mounted in /etc/tapyr deployment.yaml One replica, non-root, read-only root file system, probes on /readyz and /healthz service.yaml Port 9790: /metrics, /metrics/self, the UI and the status API pvc.yaml 1 GiB for the state store

items.title: Install
items.text:
1. Write your accounts, jobs and output in config.yaml (the README of each provider package has an example), and check it:
tapyr validate --config config.yaml
  1. Create the namespace and the Secret tapyr with the environment variables the configuration refers to ({ env: NAME }) and TAPYR_STATE_KEY, which encrypts the tokens kept in the state store. From a file of NAME=value lines, kept out of Git:
kubectl create namespace tapyr
kubectl -n tapyr create secret generic tapyr --from-env-file=tapyr.env
  1. Apply:
kubectl apply -k .
kubectl -n tapyr rollout status deploy/tapyr
kubectl -n tapyr port-forward svc/tapyr 9790:9790    # then http://127.0.0.1:9790/ui/

items.title: Operate
items.text:
• Configuration changes. The name of the ConfigMap carries a hash of config.yaml: edit the file, apply again, and the Deployment restarts with the new configuration. A restart keeps the state store, so nothing is spent twice.
  • One replica. Never scale the Deployment: a second instance would spend the same quotas without coordinating. The Recreate strategy stops the old pod before the new one opens the state store.
  • State. Keep the volume: it remembers what was already spent of the daily and monthly quotas, and the rotated tokens (every refresh of an Aruba Central token returns a new refresh token, and the previous one is no longer valid).
  • Resources. About 75 MiB of memory for 22,000 series (10,000 devices): adjust the limit to the size of your inventories.
  • Logs. kubectl -n tapyr logs deploy/tapyr, in JSON.

items.title: Scrape
items.text:
With the Prometheus Operator, a ServiceMonitor for the collected samples and the self-metrics:

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: tapyr
  namespace: tapyr
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: tapyr }
  endpoints:
    - port: http
      path: /metrics
      honorTimestamps: true
    - port: http
      path: /metrics/self

To push instead of being scraped, add a remote_write or otlp output to config.yaml (see docs/outputs.md).

items.title: systemd
items.text: tapyr.service runs Tapyr as a hardened systemd service: a dynamic user, a read-only system, no capabilities, the network and its state directory only (systemd-analyze security tapyr rates it 1.4, "OK").

items.title: Install
items.text:
The deb and rpm packages install this unit: write the configuration and the secrets as below, then sudo systemctl enable --now tapyr.

With the binary installed by hand, in /usr/local/bin/tapyr (see docs/install.md):

sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/tapyr
sudo install -m 0644 config.yaml /etc/tapyr/           # your Account, Job, Output documents
sudo install -m 0600 /dev/null /etc/tapyr/tapyr.env     # then write the secrets in it
sudo install -m 0644 tapyr.service /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now tapyr

/etc/tapyr/tapyr.env holds the environment variables the configuration refers to ({ env: NAME }), one NAME=value per line, and TAPYR_STATE_KEY, which encrypts the tokens kept in the state store:

TAPYR_MERAKI_API_KEY=...
TAPYR_STATE_KEY=...

systemd reads it as root before starting Tapyr, so it stays 0600 root:root. Tapyr reads only the *.yaml and *.yml files of /etc/tapyr, and they must be readable by the dynamic user (0644).

items.title: Operate
items.text:
systemctl status tapyr
journalctl -u tapyr -f          # JSON logs; settings.log.format: text for plain lines
sudo systemctl reload tapyr     # reload the configuration (SIGHUP)
sudo tapyr validate --config /etc/tapyr
  • Listener. Tapyr listens on 127.0.0.1:9790 by default. For a Prometheus on another host, set settings.server.listen to 0.0.0.0:9790, and protect the UI and the status API with settings.server.basicAuth or a firewall.
  • State. The state store is /var/lib/tapyr/data/tapyr.db (/var/lib/private/tapyr on disk, because of DynamicUser). It remembers what was already spent of the daily and monthly quotas, and the rotated tokens (every refresh of an Aruba Central token returns a new refresh token, and the previous one is no longer valid): back it up with the host, and do not delete it to "reset" Tapyr.
  • Provider packages. User packages go in /etc/tapyr/providers with providerPaths: [./providers] in a Settings document (relative paths are resolved against the file that declares them).
  • One instance per account. Run a single Tapyr per set of accounts: two instances polling the same accounts spend the same quotas without coordinating.

items.title: Secrets as files
items.text:
To keep the secrets out of the environment, use systemd credentials with file secrets. A drop-in (systemctl edit tapyr):

[Service]
LoadCredential=meraki-api-key:/etc/tapyr/credentials/meraki-api-key

and in the configuration:

secrets: { apiKey: { file: /run/credentials/tapyr.service/meraki-api-key } }

File secrets are read again on every reload.

items.title: aruba-central-classic
items.text:
HPE Aruba Networking Central, classic platform, REST API: access points, switches, gateways and sites of a Central account. The newer GreenLake-based Central uses another API and will be a separate package.

Validation status: tested against a real Central account (November 2026, strictly read-only): every template, the refresh of the rotating token pair, a restart resuming from the stored pair, and the daily quota headers, which matched the documented formula. The package is built from the Aruba developer hub and the official pycentral SDK, and tested in CI against a simulator that follows the shape of the real responses, rotates refresh tokens and enforces the limits below.

items.title: Coverage
items.text:
Template Endpoint Default interval Requests Metrics aruba-aps GET /monitoring/v2/aps?calculate_client_count=true 5m 1 per 1000 APs (288 a day) aruba_ap_up, aruba_ap_clients, aruba_ap_info (name, model, firmware, group, site), aruba_aps aruba-switches GET /monitoring/v1/switches 15m 1 per 1000 switches (96 a day) aruba_switch_up, aruba_switch_info (name, model, firmware, group, site, switch type) aruba-gateways GET /monitoring/v1/gateways 15m 1 per 1000 gateways (96 a day) aruba_gateway_up, aruba_gateway_info (name, model, firmware, group, site, role) aruba-sites GET /central/v2/sites 1h 1 per 1000 sites (24 a day) aruba_site_info
  • Lists are read 1000 items per page (the maximum), with calculate_total=true for the pagination.
  • The client count of each access point comes with the access point list (calculate_client_count=true), at no extra call; per-site counts are sums by site of aruba_ap_clients * on (serial) group_left (site) aruba_ap_info.
  • Measures carry the serial only; names, sites and groups are in the _info metrics. No client MAC address is collected.

items.title: Auth setup
items.text:
Aruba Central (classic) uses OAuth access tokens valid 2 hours and rotating refresh tokens valid 15 days: every refresh returns a new refresh token, and the previous one must not be used again (access token management). The aruba_central_classic auth plugin handles it:

  1. In Central, API Gateway > System Apps & Tokens (or My Apps & Tokens): add an application, note its client ID and secret, then generate and download a token pair.
  2. Give Tapyr clientId, clientSecret, refreshToken and, optionally, accessToken as secrets (see examples/aruba.yaml), and the API gateway of your cluster as baseURL (a token only works on its cluster).
  3. Set TAPYR_STATE_KEY: the rotated pair is stored in the state store, encrypted with it.

Tapyr refreshes the token 10 minutes before it expires with POST /oauth2/token?client_id=...&client_secret=...&grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=... (parameters in the query, as documented), writes the new pair to the state store before using it, and serializes refreshes per account. After a restart it resumes from the stored pair; changing the bootstrap refreshToken secret (after a reload or a restart) replaces the stored pair.

If the refresh token is rejected (400 or 401: expired after 15 days without use, revoked, or used by another tool), Tapyr stops calling the API for the account, logs an error, sets tapyr_auth_reauth_required{provider="aruba-central-classic"} to 1 and lists the account in the conditions of /readyz. Generate a new token pair and update the bootstrap secrets.

Do not share a token pair between Tapyr and another tool: the first one to refresh invalidates the refresh token of the other. A crash between a refresh answer and its storage loses the pair (the refresh is the only request in flight for the account): the account then needs a new pair.

tapyr record can run next to tapyr run: with the same configuration and TAPYR_STATE_KEY, it reads the current pair from the state store and never refreshes it. It uses the stored access token until its expiry; past it, it stops and asks to retry once tapyr run has renewed the token.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
Limit Value Source daily (quota) max(5000, 30 per Foundation device + 90 per Advanced device) calls per account and day, reset at midnight GMT; max: auto synced from X-RateLimit-Limit-day and X-RateLimit-Remaining-day (5000 until learned) Usage and rate limits second 7 calls per account per second Same page (429 when exceeded)

The daily quota is the binding constraint: favor long intervals for inventory-like jobs and check tapyr plan. Token creation through the login and authorization-code APIs is limited to one per client ID every 30 minutes; the refresh API used by the plugin has no documented limit. No Retry-After is documented for 429: Tapyr applies a 2-second penalty, growing on consecutive 429.

If other integrations use the same account, give Tapyr a share of the quota (budget.share); their consumption shows in tapyr_budget_external_usage when the headers are synced.

items.title: Simulator
items.text:
tapyr sim --provider aruba-central-classic --listen 127.0.0.1:8081

8081 is the port of the simulator under tapyr sim --all --listen-base 127.0.0.1:8081 (portOffset: 0). A synthetic account of 3 sites with 8 access points, 2 switches and a gateway each, in the shape of the responses of a real account. The simulator serves the refresh endpoint of the plugin (client sim-client / sim-client-secret, bootstrap refresh token sim-refresh-token, valid once, then rotated like Central; bootstrap access token sim-access-token), issues 2-hour access tokens, enforces 7 calls per second and the daily quota, and sends the X-RateLimit-*-day headers.

Scenario Effect default No fault quota-tight The daily quota at its floor of 5000 calls, another integration spending 150 calls an hour bad-day Another integration spends 100 calls an hour; at 1h the access tokens are revoked (one refresh); from 2h, 30% of the monitoring requests fail with 503 for 30 minutes; from 3h, slow responses (p50 1 s, p99 8 s) for an hour

items.title: Dashboard
items.text: dashboards/aruba-central-classic.json (Grafana, Prometheus data source, site variable): devices up and down, wireless clients by site and access point, switches and gateways, re-bootstrap condition, daily quota (limit, used by Tapyr and by others, remaining).

items.title: Known caveats
items.text:
• The access point list carries no uptime, and the gateway list no access point count: the package has no metric for them.
  • The role of a gateway can be empty.
  • Whether a refresh token stays valid for a while after a refresh is not documented: the plugin treats it as spent at once.
  • The CPU, memory and uptime of switches and gateways (in their lists) are not collected yet.

items.title: cisco-thousandeyes
items.text:
Cisco ThousandEyes API v7: the network results of the tests (latency, loss, jitter and health score, per test and agent), the tests and the agents of an account group.

Validation status: simulator only. The package is built from the rate limit documentation of API v7 and the official SDKs (thousandeyes-sdk-python 7.0.110: paths, parameters and fields of its generated docs), and tested against a simulator in CI; it has not been run against a real ThousandEyes account yet. A real validation needs an account group with network tests, an API token of a user with read access, one run of examples/thousandeyes.yaml, and anonymized recordings (tapyr record) compared with the fixtures. Reports are welcome.

items.title: Coverage
items.text:
Template Endpoint Default interval Requests Metrics thousandeyes-tests GET /tests 1h 1 thousandeyes_test_info (name, type), thousandeyes_test_enabled, thousandeyes_test_interval_seconds thousandeyes-agents GET /agents 15m 1 thousandeyes_agent_info (name, type, location, country), thousandeyes_agent_up (enterprise agents) thousandeyes-network-results GET /test-results/{testId}/network, one instance per enabled agent-to-server or agent-to-agent test 5m 1 per test thousandeyes_network_latency_seconds (average), thousandeyes_network_latency_min_seconds, thousandeyes_network_latency_max_seconds, thousandeyes_network_jitter_seconds, thousandeyes_network_loss_ratio, thousandeyes_network_health_score, thousandeyes_network_results_truncated
  • thousandeyes-tests is also the inventory of the network results: a job using thousandeyes-network-results alone is enough, the tests are listed implicitly.
  • Without a time window, the API returns the latest round of every agent of a test. The network samples carry the time of their round (roundId) as source timestamp: a round already sent is not sent again (deduplication), so a 5-minute job does not repeat a 10-minute round.
  • Network measures carry test_id and agent_id; names, types and locations are in the _info metrics. No IP address, hostname or serial of an agent, no target address, and no user name (createdBy, modifiedBy) is collected.
  • thousandeyes_network_health_score is from 0 to 1; the negative values of the API (error codes) are skipped.
  • One page is read per request: without a window, the latest round of every agent fits it. thousandeyes_network_results_truncated is 1 when the API reported a next page, which would mean results were not read.
  • Other test types (HTTP server, page load, web transactions, DNS, BGP, voice) have their own results endpoints: not collected yet. Endpoint agents (the endpoint experience APIs) neither.

items.title: Auth setup
items.text:
API v7 authenticates with a bearer token (Authorization: Bearer <token>).

  1. In ThousandEyes, create an API token for a user whose role can read the tests and the agents of the account group (the user API tokens of the user settings).
  2. Give Tapyr the token as the apiToken secret (see examples/thousandeyes.yaml).
  3. Optional: the accountGroupId param selects the account group (the aid parameter of the API); without it, the API uses the default account group of the token's user. The account group IDs are listed by GET /account-groups.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
Limit Value Source organization (quota) 240 requests a minute per organization, the minute starting at the first request of a batch; max: auto synced from X-Organization-Rate-Limit-Limit, -Remaining and -Reset (240 until learned) Rate limits
  • The documented example shows X-Organization-Rate-Limit-Limit: 20 where the text says 240: the max is learned from the header.
  • The window starts at the first request, not on the clock: the reset header (the epoch of the next rollover) keeps the window of Tapyr on the one of the API, and the remaining header keeps the count exact in between. Tested in the engine against a model of this API: no 429, even for bursts of the whole budget (spec 04, Header sync). Do not remove the reset header from the sync block.
  • Exceeded, the API answers 429, without Retry-After; the documentation says to wait for the reset, which the quota does.
  • The limit is per organization, shared by every user, token and integration of it: other integrations show in tapyr_budget_external_usage; give Tapyr a share (budget.share) when they need room. Instant tests (24 calls a minute) and template deployments have limits of their own; the package uses neither.

With the defaults, an account group with 50 network tests spends about 10 requests a minute (one per test every 5 minutes, plus one for the tests every hour and one for the agents every 15 minutes), far from the 240 of the limit.

items.title: Simulator
items.text:
tapyr sim --provider cisco-thousandeyes --listen 127.0.0.1:8087

8087 is the port of the simulator under tapyr sim --all --listen-base 127.0.0.1:8081 (portOffset: 6). A synthetic account group of 5 tests (3 agent-to-server, one of them disabled, 1 agent-to-agent, 1 http-server) and 5 agents (3 cloud, 2 enterprise), under /v7, in the response shape of the SDK docs. It accepts the token sim-thousandeyes-token, enforces the organization limit and sends the three headers.

Known gaps of the simulator: its windows are aligned on the clock (not on the first request), and it sends the reset header as seconds until the reset (the API sends an epoch). Tapyr reads both forms.

Scenario Effect default No fault quota-tight The limit at 20 requests a minute (the documented example), another integration spending 5 of them org-burst As quota-tight, and the other integration bursts through the whole minute at 29, 59 and 89 minutes: Tapyr's requests of those minutes get 429, its jobs keep their intervals bad-day From 1h, slow responses (p50 700 ms, p99 4 s) for an hour; from 2h, 30% of the test results requests fail with 502 for 30 minutes; at 4h, a 10-minute outage

items.title: Dashboard
items.text: dashboards/cisco-thousandeyes.json (Grafana, Prometheus data source, test variable): tests, enterprise agents offline, highest loss and latency, lowest health score, average latency, loss and jitter by test, the worst paths by loss, the agents, and the organization limit of the current minute (limit, used by Tapyr and by others).

items.title: Known caveats
items.text:
• Simulator-validated only (see above). The fields come from the generated docs of the official SDKs.
  • Only the network results of agent-to-server and agent-to-agent tests; bidirectional agent-to-agent tests are read with the default direction of the API.

items.title: example-sim
items.text:
A vendor-neutral example provider, used for development, tests and demos, and the reference package that new packages copy: small, served by the built-in simulator, every feature exercised (four pagination styles, a three-level discovery chain, quota headers, scenarios).

Validation status: simulator only, by design. All fixture data is synthetic.

items.title: Coverage
items.text:
Template Endpoint Default interval Requests Metrics example-sim-sites GET /sites (offset pagination, 2 items per page) 1h 1 per 2 sites example_site_devices, example_site_info example-sim-devices GET /devices (Link header pagination, 2 items per page) 5m 1 per 2 devices example_device_up, example_device_clients, example_device_received_bytes_total, example_device_info, example_devices example-sim-networks GET /sites/{siteId}/networks, one instance per site (page pagination, 2 items per page) 30m 1 per 2 networks of a site example_network_info example-sim-network-devices GET /sites/{siteId}/networks/{networkId}/devices, one instance per network (cursor pagination, 2 items per page, next cursor in X-Next-Cursor) 5m 1 per 2 devices of a network example_network_device_up
  • example-sim-sites is also an inventory (role: both, one item per site), example-sim-networks fans out over it and is the inventory of example-sim-network-devices: a three-level discovery chain. A job using example-sim-network-devices alone is enough, the two parents are instantiated implicitly.
  • example_devices is the number of devices returned by the last run.

items.title: Auth setup
items.text: Bearer token from the apiKey secret. The simulator accepts sim-api-key.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
Limit Value Source account-rate 10 requests per second per account Assumed, example only concurrency 4 concurrent requests per Tapyr instance Assumed, example only daily (quota) max: auto, synced from X-RateLimit-Limit-Day and X-RateLimit-Remaining-Day (5000 until learned), reset at 00:00 UTC Assumed, example only

The limits are illustrative and not sourced from any real API. The simulator enforces them (429 with Retry-After) and sends the X-RateLimit-Limit-Day and X-RateLimit-Remaining-Day headers.

items.title: Simulator
items.text:
tapyr sim --provider example-sim --listen 127.0.0.1:8081

Unlike the other packages, the example uses 8081 standalone, not the port it gets from tapyr sim --all --listen-base 127.0.0.1:8081 (8082, portOffset: 1): the default baseURL of the provider, examples/example-sim.yaml and examples/config expect it there.

The simulator serves static fixtures under /api/v1: 3 sites, 5 devices, and the networks of each site with their devices.

Scenario Effect default No fault quota-tight The daily quota drops to 600 calls bad-day Another client consumes 60 calls per hour; from 2h to 2h20, 30% of /devices requests fail with 503 quota-jump A daily quota of 2000 calls; another client spends 300 of them between 12h and 12h10, then 600 more between 18h and 18h10 inventory-change After 2h, site-c is closed, site-d opens, site-a loses a network and site-b gains one 
tapyr sim --provider example-sim --scenario quota-tight --time-scale 60

items.title: Dashboard
items.text: dashboards/example-sim.json (Grafana, Prometheus data source, site variable): devices online and offline, clients, received throughput, inventory, devices per site, network devices online, daily quota (limit, used by Tapyr and by others, remaining).

items.title: Known caveats
items.text: • Not a real API: the limits and payloads only exist in the simulator.

items.title: juniper-mist
items.text:
Juniper Mist cloud REST API: access points, switches and gateways (WAN edge) of a Mist organization, their sites and alarms.

Validation status: simulator only. The package is built from the Mist documentation (rate limits, pagination, regional clouds) and the Mist OpenAPI description (2610.1.0, November 2026), and tested against a simulator in CI; it has not been run against a real Mist organization yet. A real validation needs an organization, an organization API token with a read-only role, one run of examples/mist.yaml, and anonymized recordings (tapyr record) compared with the fixtures. Reports are welcome.

items.title: Coverage
items.text:
Template Endpoint Default interval Requests Metrics mist-devices GET /api/v1/orgs/{orgId}/stats/devices?type=all 5m 1 per 1000 devices (12 an hour) mist_device_up, mist_device_uptime_seconds, mist_device_clients, mist_device_cpu_usage_ratio, mist_device_memory_usage_ratio, mist_device_info (name, type, model, serial, version, site) mist-sites GET /api/v1/orgs/{orgId}/stats/sites 15m 1 per 1000 sites (4 an hour) mist_site_devices and mist_site_devices_connected (by type: ap, switch, gateway), mist_site_clients, mist_site_info (name, country code, time zone) mist-alarms GET /api/v1/orgs/{orgId}/alarms/count?distinct=severity&duration=1d 15m 1 (4 an hour) mist_alarms_last_day (by severity: critical, warn, info)
  • Organization-level endpoints only: the cost does not grow with the number of sites, as the Mist documentation recommends for large deployments.
  • Device measures carry the device mac (the identifier of a Mist device), sites the site_id; names are in the _info metrics. No client MAC or IP address is collected.
  • mist_device_clients exists for access points only. mist_device_cpu_usage_ratio comes from cpu_util on access points and from the idle share of cpu_stat on switches and gateways; mist_device_memory_usage_ratio from mem_used_kb / mem_total_kb on access points and from memory_stat.usage on switches and gateways.
  • mist_alarms_last_day is a rolling count of the alarms raised over the last 24 hours, acknowledged ones included.
  • Lists are read 1000 items per page (limit and page, the documented maximum). The pagination stops on the first page shorter than 1000 items: when a list holds an exact multiple of 1000, one more (empty) page is requested.

items.title: Auth setup
items.text:
Mist API tokens are sent as Authorization: Token <key> (the header auth type with format: "Token {value}").

  1. In the Mist portal, Organization > Settings > API Token: create an organization token with a read-only role (Observer). It is not bound to a user and only works for its organization.
  2. Give Tapyr the token as the apiToken secret, the organization ID (Organization > Settings) as the orgId param, and the API host of your cloud as baseURL (see examples/mist.yaml).

A user token works too, but its rate limit is shared with every token of the user and with their portal sessions (see below).

items.title: Regional clouds
items.text:
The API host depends on the cloud of the organization: replace manage by api in the address of the portal (endpoints by global region).

Cloud baseURL Global 01 (default) https://api.mist.com Global 02 https://api.gc1.mist.com Global 03 https://api.ac2.mist.com Global 04 https://api.gc2.mist.com Global 05 https://api.gc4.mist.com EMEA 01 https://api.eu.mist.com EMEA 02 https://api.gc3.mist.com EMEA 03 https://api.ac6.mist.com EMEA 04 https://api.gc6.mist.com APAC 01 https://api.ac5.mist.com APAC 02 https://api.gc5.mist.com APAC 03 https://api.gc7.mist.com

items.title: Limits
items.text:
Limit Value Source hourly (quota) 5000 calls per hour, reset at the hourly boundary (aligned on the clock, UTC), per API token (scope: credential) API rate limiting, Org API token, RESTful API overview
  • An organization token is limited on its own: another token reaching its limit does not affect it. A user token counts for the whole user account, other tokens and portal logins included: Tapyr only sees its own calls, so give it a dedicated organization token, or a share of the quota (budget.share) when the token is shared.
  • Exceeded, the API answers 429 (REST API HTTP response codes). No Retry-After and no rate-limit headers are documented: Tapyr applies a 60-second penalty, growing on consecutive 429.
  • No per-second or concurrency limit is documented, and none is declared.
  • The login API is rate-limited after three failures; the package does not use it.

With the defaults, an organization of up to 1000 devices and 1000 sites spends about 20 calls an hour (12 for the devices, 4 for the sites, 4 for the alarms), far from the 5000 of the quota; each further 1000 devices adds 12 calls an hour.

items.title: Simulator
items.text:
tapyr sim --provider juniper-mist --listen 127.0.0.1:8086

8086 is the port of the simulator under tapyr sim --all --listen-base 127.0.0.1:8081 (portOffset: 5). A synthetic organization (orgId free) of 3 sites with 6 access points, 2 switches and a gateway each, in the response shape of the Mist OpenAPI description. It accepts the token sim-mist-token (as Authorization: Token sim-mist-token) and enforces the hourly quota. It does not send X-Page-Total.

Scenario Effect default No fault quota-tight The token is shared with a script spending 4990 calls an hour: about 10 calls are left, fewer than the defaults need bad-day From 1h, slow responses (p50 800 ms, p99 5 s) for an hour; from 2h, 30% of the statistics requests fail with 503 for 30 minutes; at 4h, a 10-minute outage

items.title: Dashboard
items.text: dashboards/juniper-mist.json (Grafana, Prometheus data source, site variable): devices connected and disconnected, wireless clients, alarms of the last 24 hours by severity, clients and disconnected devices by site, busiest access points, CPU and memory of the busiest devices, hourly quota (limit, used by Tapyr and by others, remaining).

items.title: Known caveats
items.text:
• Simulator-validated only (see above). Paths and fields come from the Mist OpenAPI description, a secondary source: the official API reference cannot be read without a browser.
  • The device and site statistics carry more than the package collects (radio, port and interface statistics, WAN uplinks): not collected yet.
  • The alarm counts are organization-wide: the site variable of the dashboard does not filter them.

items.title: meraki-dashboard
items.text:
Cisco Meraki Dashboard API v1: device availability, appliance uplinks and wireless clients of every organization the API key can read.

Validation status: tested against a real Dashboard (a DevNet sandbox organization, November 2026: every template, with 1 network and 4 devices: appliance, switch, access point and camera), and against a synthetic simulator in CI. The package is built from the official documentation and OpenAPI description (v1.75.1). The appliance of the sandbox reports no uplink, so meraki-appliance-uplink-statuses was checked on the shape of the response only: reports from organizations with active uplinks are welcome.

items.title: Coverage
items.text:
All metric jobs use organization-wide endpoints: one request per organization and job (one page per 1000 items), whatever the number of networks and devices.

Template Endpoint Default interval Requests Metrics meraki-organizations GET /organizations 1h 1 per account meraki_organization_api_enabled, meraki_organization_info; inventory of the other jobs meraki-networks GET /organizations/{organizationId}/networks 1h 1 per organization (per 1000 items) meraki_network_info (name, product types, time zone) meraki-devices GET /organizations/{organizationId}/devices 1h 1 per organization (per 1000 items) meraki_device_info (name, model, firmware, product type, network) meraki-device-availabilities GET /organizations/{organizationId}/devices/availabilities 5m 1 per organization (per 1000 items) meraki_device_up (online or alerting), meraki_device_alerting meraki-appliance-uplink-statuses GET /organizations/{organizationId}/appliance/uplink/statuses 5m 1 per organization (per 1000 items) meraki_appliance_uplink_active, meraki_appliance_uplink_up (active or ready), per appliance and interface meraki-wireless-client-counts GET /organizations/{organizationId}/wireless/clients/overview/byDevice 5m 1 per organization (per 1000 items) meraki_wireless_device_clients (clients connected now, per access point)
  • meraki-device-availabilities replaces devices/statuses, deprecated in October 2024 (deprecated operations); Meraki refreshes availabilities every 5 minutes, hence the default interval.
  • Measures carry organization_id, network_id and serial, and meraki_device_up and meraki_device_alerting also carry product_type (appliance, switch, wireless...); names, models and firmware are in the _info metrics. No client MAC address is collected.
  • Uplink IP addresses are not exposed.

items.title: Auth setup
items.text: Create an API key in the Dashboard (My profile > API access), ideally for a read-only administrator of the organizations to monitor, and give it to Tapyr as the apiKey secret. It is sent as Authorization: Bearer (authorization). For regional Dashboards, set the baseURL param (https://api.meraki.ca/api/v1, https://api.meraki.cn/api/v1, https://api.meraki.in/api/v1, https://api.gov-meraki.com/api/v1). The Dashboard may redirect a request to the shard of the organization (n123.meraki.com): the package allows redirects to the hosts of the Meraki domains (redirects.hosts), and Tapyr sends the key there too, each redirect being a request reserved in the budget.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
Limit Value Source org-rate 10 requests per second per organization, burst 20 (10 extra in the first second), on the requests carrying organizationId Rate limit: "up to 10 requests per second per organization", "an extra 10 requests in the first second", shared across all API applications of the organization ip-rate 100 requests per second per Tapyr instance Same page: "up to 100 requests per second from each source IP address" ip-concurrency 10 concurrent requests per Tapyr instance Assumed: not documented officially, commonly reported by the community

429 responses carry Retry-After, honored by the budget engine. There is no daily quota: the per-organization rate is the constraint, and it is shared with the other applications using the API on the same organizations (the official SDK keeps 1 request per second for them). The example gives Tapyr half of it (budget: { share: 0.5, scaleRates: true }).

Quota maths with the defaults, one page per 1000 items: each organization costs 3 requests per 5 minutes (meraki-device-availabilities, meraki-appliance-uplink-statuses, meraki-wireless-client-counts), 36 an hour, plus 2 an hour (meraki-networks, meraki-devices); the account adds 1 an hour (meraki-organizations). An account with 2 organizations sends 77 requests an hour, far below the per-organization rate: the rate matters for bursts and for the share left to other applications. tapyr plan shows the projection.

items.title: Simulator
items.text:
tapyr sim --provider meraki-dashboard --listen 127.0.0.1:8083

8083 is the port of the simulator under tapyr sim --all --listen-base 127.0.0.1:8081 (portOffset: 2). A synthetic Dashboard of 2 organizations, each with 4 networks of 10 devices (an MX appliance, three MS switches, six MR access points), generated from a seed. Statuses flap every 5 minutes, client counts and appliance uplinks move over simulated time. The simulator accepts the key sim-meraki-key, paginates with Link headers and enforces the limits above.

Scenario Effect default No fault quota-tight No daily quota on Meraki: other applications spend most of the per-organization rate, a third of the organization requests get 429 bad-day From 1h, slow responses (p50 600 ms, p99 4 s) for an hour; from 2h, 25% of the organization requests fail with 502 for 30 minutes; at 4h, a 10-minute outage

items.title: Dashboard
items.text: dashboards/meraki-dashboard.json (Grafana, Prometheus data source, organization and network variables): devices up and down, alerting, appliance uplinks and networks on a backup uplink, wireless clients, API requests and 429 (Tapyr self-metrics).
