• Every reference resolves (account -> provider, template -> provider, job -> account, job -> template, forEach -> template | job, outputs -> output, selfMetrics.outputs -> output). Provider names resolve against the configuration, the providerPaths packages and the built-in packages.
  • Names are unique per kind; at most one Settings document; at most one prometheus output.
  • Discovery graph is acyclic; maximum depth 4 (at most 4 fan-out levels from the root inventory job to the deepest child; a job using a template shares the level of its template).
  • A job template's provider matches the job account's provider.
  • Accounts provide every required param and secret, and no undeclared one.
  • Template fields parse as Go templates using only the allowed functions.
  • All CEL expressions compile and type-check against the job's environment (see 06-mapping-and-outputs.md).
  • Every variable used in a path template is provided by forEach.vars or the account params.
  • Scope dimensions var:<name> refer to variables available in the requests the limit applies to.
  • Metric names follow Prometheus naming rules; label names are valid; a metric name has a single type across all jobs.
  • budget.share in (0, 1]. retryReserve in [0%, 50%].
  • Required secrets resolve at startup (validate --check-secrets checks them offline).

items.title: 04 - Budget engine
items.text: The budget engine is the heart of Tapyr. Its contract: no request leaves Tapyr unless every applicable limit allows it, and quota is spent according to priorities, with a reserve for retries.

items.title: Concepts
items.text:
• Limit: a constraint declared in a provider definition (spec.limits).
  • Scope: the key that partitions a limit. A limit with scope [account, var:organizationId] is a separate counter for every (account, organization) pair.
  • Scope key: the concrete value of a scope for a request, e.g. acme-meraki/org=549236.
  • Request descriptor: what the executor passes to the engine for each request (provider, account, target, credential, templated endpoint, variables, job, priority, retry flag, auth-request flag).
  • Reservation: a grant to send one request, possibly obtained after waiting. Reservations are released (concurrency) and settled (quota sync) after the response.

items.title: rate - token bucket
items.text:
- name: org-rate
  kind: rate
  rate: 10/s          # refill rate
  burst: 10           # bucket capacity (default: rate per second, minimum 1)
  scope: { by: [account, "var:organizationId"] }

In-memory. Requests wait for a token (bounded by the request's deadline). When the burst is 2 or more, a request also leaves one token in the bucket: requests leave at the pace of the limit but reach the provider with a varying latency, and a provider bucket of the same size would refuse one that arrives slightly early. The token in hand keeps the provider's bucket one token ahead, which absorbs up to one interval of jitter; the sustained rate is unchanged and a burst is one request shorter. The simulator enforces the full burst.

items.title: concurrency
items.text:
- name: ip-concurrency
  kind: concurrency
  max: 10
  scope: { by: [instance] }

In-memory semaphore. Released when the response is fully read or the request fails.

items.title: quota - fixed window
items.text:
- name: daily
  kind: quota
  max: 5000                 # or "auto" (learned from headers, see Header sync)
  # initialMax: 5000        # required with max: auto, used until a header is seen
  window:
    period: day             # minute | hour | day | week | month
    resetAt: "00:00"        # for day/week/month
    timezone: UTC           # IANA name
    weekStart: monday       # for week
    monthDay: 1             # for month
  scope: { by: [account] }
  sync:
    limitHeader: X-RateLimit-Limit-day
    remainingHeader: X-RateLimit-Remaining-day
    resetHeader: ""         # optional: header carrying reset time (epoch seconds or delta)

Persistent. Window boundaries are computed from the calendar in the declared timezone (DST-safe).

  • Defaults: resetAt: "00:00", timezone: UTC, weekStart: monday, monthDay: 1.
  • resetAt is HH:MM (24h). A reset time that does not exist on a given day (DST gap) is normalized forward, following Go's time.Date semantics.
  • monthDay is 1 to 31; in shorter months the window resets on the last day of the month.
  • minute and hour windows are aligned on the clock in the declared timezone.
  • max: auto requires initialMax (a conservative value used until the first limit header is observed) and sync.limitHeader.

items.title: quota - rolling window
items.text:
- name: rolling-24h
  kind: quota
  max: 10000
  window: { rolling: 24h }
  scope: { by: [credential] }

Persistent. Implemented with per-minute buckets (bounded memory, 1-minute precision).

items.title: Applicability filters
items.text:
A limit applies to a request only if its scope can be resolved and its filters match:

appliesTo:
  endpoints: ["/organizations/**"]      # glob on templated path
  methods: [GET]
  requestsWithVar: organizationId       # only if this variable is set
  authRequests: include                 # include (default) | only | exclude, see Auth limits

Endpoint globs match the templated path segment by segment: * matches within one segment, ** matches zero or more whole segments. /organizations/* matches /organizations/{organizationId} but not /organizations/{organizationId}/networks; /organizations/** matches both.

items.title: Auth limits
items.text:
Token requests (OAuth, login) are budgeted too. appliesTo.authRequests selects which requests a limit counts:

  • include (default): both regular and auth requests,
  • only: auth requests only (for example a dedicated limit on token creations per hour),
  • exclude: regular requests only.

Without a dedicated limit, auth requests therefore count against every generic limit that does not exclude them.

items.title: Scope dimensions
items.text:
Dimension Meaning instance The whole Tapyr process (approximates "per source IP") provider All accounts of the provider in this process account One Account target One target of a multi-target Account credential One credential set (accounts sharing the same secret values share this key; computed as a salted hash, never logged; the salt is generated randomly once and stored in the state store so ledger keys stay stable across restarts) endpoint The templated path var:<name> Value of a request variable (from discovery or params)

An empty by is equivalent to [instance].

items.title: Reservation algorithm
items.text:
For each request:

  1. Collect applicable limits and compute scope keys.
  2. Reject immediately if:
  3. a scope is penalized (after a 429 with Retry-After) and the penalty outlasts the request deadline,
  4. a quota scope is exhausted for the current window (taking budget share and reserves into account),
  5. the account's circuit breaker is open. The refusal carries a reason (quota_exhausted, penalized, circuit_open, deadline).
  6. Otherwise, acquire every applicable limit atomically under the engine lock: quota units (check and increment), concurrency slots and rate tokens. When a concurrency slot or a rate token is not available, the request acquires nothing and waits; if the wait would exceed the deadline, it is refused with deadline.
  7. Return the reservation.

Waiting is priority-aware: when several requests wait on the same scope, higher priority goes first (critical > high > normal > low), FIFO within a priority.

items.title: Quota accounting with share and reserve
items.text:
For a quota limit with effective maximum M (after header learning) and account budget.share s:

  • Usable budget: U = floor(M * s).
  • Retry reserve: R = floor(U * retryReserve) (global setting, default 10%).
  • Normal requests may consume up to U - R.
  • Retries may consume up to U.
  • critical jobs may dip into the reserve for normal requests once the normal budget is exhausted (they keep running, retries for others stop first).
  • When a scope key is shared by several accounts with different shares (scopes without account or target, such as instance, provider or credential), s is the smallest share among the accounts contributing to that key.

items.title: Header sync
items.text:
After each response, the engine reads the sync headers of every applicable quota limit:

  • Learn the limit: if max: auto (or if the header disagrees with the declared max), the effective max becomes the header value. Disagreement is logged once per window and exposed as a metric.
  • Learn the remaining: with M the effective max (whole quota, as reported by the provider), U = floor(M * s) the usable budget, c Tapyr's own consumption in the window and r_obs the observed remaining (whole quota):
  • observed total consumption: C_obs = M - r_obs,
  • external consumption (other tools using the same quota): external = max(0, C_obs - c), exposed as tapyr_budget_external_usage,
  • Tapyr's remaining budget: remaining = min(U - c, r_obs). Tapyr never exceeds its share and never exceeds what is actually left.
  • Reset: if a reset header is declared, it overrides the computed window end.
  • Windows that start at the first request (ThousandEyes: one minute "from the first request in a batch") need no window option: with a reset header, every response sets the end of the window to the provider's, so the engine rolls when the provider does and its next window, opened by the next request, matches the provider's; the remaining header keeps the count exact in between. Without a reset header, the engine rolls on the clock while the window of the provider still runs, and a burst sent right after, before any response, can exceed it: declare the reset header for such providers (TestFirstRequestWindows covers both).

Headers are matched case-insensitively. Missing headers are ignored silently.

items.title: 429 handling
items.text:
When a response matches errors.rateLimited:

  • Determine the penalty duration from Retry-After (seconds or HTTP date), else from the provider default (errors.rateLimited.defaultPenalty, default 2s), with exponential growth on consecutive 429s for the same scope (cap 10 minutes).
  • Apply the penalty to the narrowest scope among applicable limits by default, or to all applicable scopes if errors.rateLimited.penalize: all.
  • If the response carries quota headers showing remaining = 0 for a quota limit, mark that quota scope exhausted until window end.
  • Count tapyr_budget_rate_limited_total with the limit name. An unexpected 429 (no internal limit predicted exhaustion) is also counted as tapyr_budget_unexpected_429_total: it means the provider definition is wrong or the quota is shared.

items.title: Ledger persistence
items.text:
• Quota counters are persisted: (limit, scope_key, window_start) -> used, observed_remaining, observed_max, updated_at.
  • Rolling windows persist per-minute buckets for their duration.
  • On startup, current-window counters are loaded. Expired windows are discarded.
  • Flush cadence: every 5 seconds and on shutdown. The engine tolerates losing the last seconds (header sync corrects).
  • A flush writes only what changed since the previous successful one: the counters that moved and the minute buckets added, changed or gone (a daily window holds up to 1440 of them, and one or two change between flushes). The first flush of a process writes every entry in full, replacing the buckets a previous process left; a failed flush is written again in full by the next.

items.title: Planner
items.text: The planner turns desired intervals into effective intervals that fit every quota.

items.title: Inputs
items.text:
• Jobs with desired interval, priority, fan-out (number of child instances, from inventory cache or estimate), estimated requests per run (pages, from run history: rolling median of the last 20 runs; else estimate.pagesPerRun; else 1), retry overhead estimate (rolling ratio, default 5%).
  • Quota limits with usable budget for the current window and time remaining in the window.
  • Rate limits (to check feasibility of bursts: a run's requests must fit in the interval at the limit's rate).

items.title: Algorithm
items.text:
1. For each quota scope, compute the projected consumption per window of every job contributing to it: calls_per_run * fanout * runs_per_window.
  2. If the sum fits U - R, effective intervals equal desired intervals.
  3. Otherwise, stretch intervals starting from the lowest priority class: within a class, apply a common multiplier k >= 1 to all jobs of that class contributing to the scope, choose the smallest k that makes the sum fit (or stretch up to settings.budget.maxStretch, default 12x, then move to the next class).
  4. critical jobs are never stretched. If critical jobs alone do not fit, the plan is infeasible: validate and plan report an error, run starts anyway with a loud warning and the status API flags it.
  5. A job contributing to several quota scopes takes the largest stretch required by any of them.
  6. Mid-window replanning (every replanInterval, on reload, on inventory change, on header-learned max change, and when the current plan is projected to exhaust a quota before its reset, see Projections): recompute using the remaining budget and the remaining time in the window, so a burst of failures in the morning tightens the afternoon instead of exhausting the quota. The remaining budget is min(U - c, r_obs) (see Header sync), less the reserve, less the consumption of other clients projected to the end of a calendar window at their pace so far (external * time_left / time_elapsed, the elapsed time counting as at least 1/24 of the window): another integration sharing the quota keeps spending until the reset. A fixed window shorter than replanInterval (a one-minute window) is planned over a full window instead (U - R, as offline): a plan paces several of them, what is left of the current one says nothing of the next, and a minute window exhausted by a 429 or by another client would otherwise stretch every job for a whole replan interval. The engine still refuses what the current window cannot take until its reset.
  7. Rate-limit feasibility: if a run's estimated calls cannot complete within its interval given applicable rate limits, the interval is stretched to the minimum feasible value.

items.title: Outputs
items.text:
For each job: desired interval, effective interval, stretch factor, contributing scopes, projected calls per window. For each quota scope: budget, projected consumption, projected exhaustion time (if any), feasibility.

The same planner code runs offline in tapyr plan, which can take inventory size hints (--fanout meraki-organizations=3) when no inventory cache exists.

items.title: Projections
items.text: For each quota scope of a fixed window, the projected exhaustion time (tapyr_budget_exhaustion_eta_seconds, absent if not projected to exhaust) extrapolates the consumption rate since the window start.

items.title: Replan on projection
items.text:
Between two replanInterval, the collector checks that the current plan still fits (settings.budget.replanOnProjection, on by default):

  • The check follows every completed run: its requests counted against the quotas, and its responses reported their remaining. It runs at most once a minute; a run ending within the minute is checked with the next one, so no timer is added.
  • The check projects the consumption of the current effective intervals until the end of every quota window (planner.Evaluate, same inputs as the online plan) and compares it with the remaining budget of the online plan (step 6 of the algorithm, external consumption projected to the reset included). Without quota headers, it only sees Tapyr's own consumption: more pages or retries than planned.
  • A scope whose projection exceeds its budget by more than 10% triggers a replan at once, at most once every 5 minutes per scope. The new plan fits the budget exactly; a later jump of external consumption crosses the 10% again.
  • A scope still infeasible after its replan (maximum stretch reached, critical jobs alone over budget) is disarmed until its projection fits its budget again, so that a plan that cannot fit never replans in a loop.
  • Only a tightening triggers it: a relaxation waits for the next replanInterval.

Every plan computation counts in tapyr_plan_recomputations_total{reason}: start, reload, interval, limit_learned, inventory or projection.

items.title: Implementation notes
items.text:
Decisions taken when implementing the engine:

  • Single engine lock. All limit state lives behind one mutex. API polling volumes are low enough, and a single lock makes multi-limit acquisition trivially atomic (no partial acquisition, no lock ordering).
  • Waiting. A request that cannot acquire every applicable limit registers as a waiter and sleeps until a limit is released, a token refills or a penalty ends (timers on the injected clock), or its deadline. A waiter may acquire only when no waiter of higher priority (or of the same priority and older) is waiting on one of its scope keys. Waiters hold nothing while they wait, so there is no deadlock.
  • Deadline. When the next token of a rate limit or the end of a penalty comes after the request deadline, the request is refused at once with deadline instead of waiting in vain.
  • Quota counting. Quota units are counted when the reservation is granted, not when the response arrives: a request that fails still consumed provider quota.
  • Remaining after an observation. r_obs is valid at the time of the response that carried it. Until the next observation, the engine uses r_obs - (c_now - c_obs), where c_obs is Tapyr's consumption when r_obs was observed.
  • Reset header. A value greater than 1e9 is an epoch in seconds; otherwise it is a delay in seconds.
  • Circuit breaker. The breakers live in the engine (it refuses with circuit_open); the executor reports successes and transient failures.
  • Credential key. HMAC-SHA256(salt, secret values), hex-truncated to 16 characters; the salt is stored in the state store.
  • Enforcer mode (simulator). The same limit evaluation answers, without waiting, whether a request is allowed now; otherwise the simulator answers 429 with Retry-After (time to the next token, end of the penalty or end of the quota window). Server-side scope keys: account, target and credential map to the presented credential, instance and provider to the whole simulator, endpoint to the route path, var:<name> to the route variable.
  • Timeline. Every quota scope keeps its consumption per bucket (1 minute for windows up to one day, 1 hour beyond) for the current and the previous window, for the status API. Fixed windows persist the buckets of the current window in ledger_minutes, as rolling windows already do.
  • Observer. The engine reports grants (with the wait), refusals and rate-limited responses to an optional observer, the source of the budget self-metrics.

items.title: Testing requirements
items.text:
• Fake clock for everything. Daily windows across DST changes, month boundaries, leap years, timezone offsets.
  • Property tests: under random request streams, no limit is ever exceeded.
  • Concurrency tests with the race detector: no partial acquisition, no deadlock with overlapping scopes.
  • Planner golden tests: given inputs, expected effective intervals.
  • Simulation test (with the simulator, accelerated fake clock): 24 simulated hours, undersized quota, verify priorities and zero quota-related 429s.

items.title: Auth
items.text:
All auth types implement one interface:

type Authenticator interface {
    // Decorate adds credentials to the request, obtaining or refreshing tokens if needed.
    Decorate(ctx context.Context, req *http.Request) error
    // OnAuthFailure is called on a response classified as authFailed.
    // It returns true if the request should be retried once after re-authentication.
    OnAuthFailure(ctx context.Context, resp *http.Response) (retry bool, err error)
}

Token requests issued by authenticators go through the budget engine with authRequest: true.

items.title: Declarative types
items.text: Type Config Notes none - header name, value (literal or secret), format (optional, {value} replaced by the value) Static API key header, e.g. X-Cisco-Meraki-API-Key, or Authorization: Token <key> with format: "Token {value}" bearer token (secret) Authorization: Bearer <token> basic username, password oauth2_client_credentials tokenURL, clientId, clientSecret, scopes, audience, extraParams, authStyle (header or body) Token cached until expires_in - skew; persisted session_login see below Generic login flow returning a token or cookie

items.title: session_login
items.text:
For APIs that require posting credentials to obtain a session token (e.g. Teltonika RutOS).

auth:
  type: session_login
  sessionLogin:
    request:
      method: POST
      path: /api/login
      body:                                   # JSON body, values are CEL or secret refs
        username: { secret: username }
        password: { secret: password }
    token: "response.body.data.token"         # CEL, extracts the token
    expiresIn: "has(response.body.data.expires) ? duration(string(response.body.data.expires) + 's') : duration('300s')"
    apply:
      header: Authorization
      format: "Bearer {token}"                # or apply.cookie: <name>
    refreshBefore: 30s
    perTarget: true                           # one session per target (multi-target accounts)
    logout: { path: /api/logout }             # optional, closes replaced sessions

On authFailed, the session is invalidated and the request retried once after a new login.

items.title: Plugins (Go)
items.text:
Reserved for flows that cannot be expressed declaratively. Registered by name in internal/auth/plugins and selected with auth.type: plugin, auth.plugin.name: <name>. The plugin receives auth.plugin.config (free-form in the core schema) and validates it at compile time.

aruba_central_classic: Aruba Central (classic) uses OAuth access tokens with a limited lifetime and rotating refresh tokens (each refresh returns a new refresh token, the previous one becomes invalid). Requirements:

  • Bootstrap from an initial access token and refresh token provided as secrets (generated in the Central UI), or from client credentials plus an initial refresh token.
  • Refresh proactively before expiry; persist the new token pair in the state store before using it (crash-safety: losing a rotated refresh token means manual re-bootstrap).
  • Serialize refreshes per account (never two concurrent refreshes).
  • If the stored token pair is newer than the bootstrap secrets, the stored pair wins. A changed bootstrap secret (detected by hash) overrides the stored pair.
  • Expose its refreshes in tapyr_auth_token_requests_total{result} and a health condition when re-bootstrap is required (tapyr_auth_reauth_required).
  • Verified behavior: see Implementation notes below.

items.title: Request building
items.text:
• path is a template with {var} placeholders resolved from variables (discovery vars, account params, target params). Values are URL-path-escaped.
  • query values are Values: literal strings, CEL expressions ({ expr: "..." }) or secret references ({ secret: name }, redacted everywhere). An expression that returns null omits the parameter, for an optional account param: { expr: "default(account.params.accountGroupId, dyn(null))" }; an empty string is sent as such.
  • headers merge provider defaults, template, then job (job wins).
  • body (for POST-based query APIs such as GraphQL) is supported: JSON with CEL-evaluated values. Tapyr remains read-only: POST is allowed only for queries, declared explicitly with readOnly: true in the template, and never retried unless idempotent: true.

items.title: Redirects
items.text: The HTTP clients never follow a redirect by themselves: a redirect followed inside the client would be a request outside the budget engine, and it would carry the credentials to the host of the Location. The executor follows a redirect (3xx with a Location, 304 excepted) as a new request of its own: a reservation, the credentials of the account, and a request counted in the run. It does so only within the origin of the request (scheme, host and port), or to a host listed by the provider in redirects.hosts (a host name, or *. and a domain), never from https to another scheme, and at most 5 times in a row. 307 and 308 keep the method and the body; the other redirects become a GET without body. Any other redirect fails the request as a client error naming the host. Token and login requests and the push outputs do not follow redirects at all.

items.title: Pagination
items.text:
Every pagination type supports maxPages (default 100, hard safety cap) and contributes each page as one budgeted request.

Type Config Stop condition none - single request offset offsetParam, limitParam, pageSize, start (default 0), stop (CEL, optional), total (CEL, optional) stop true, or offset >= total, or fewer items than pageSize page pageParam, sizeParam, pageSize, start (default 1), stop, total same logic with page numbers link_header pageSizeParam, pageSize, rel (default next) no rel=next link (RFC 8288). Links are followed only when they keep the scheme, host and port of the base URL, so credentials are never sent elsewhere cursor cursor (CEL extracting next cursor from response), param (query param name) or header, pageSizeParam, pageSize cursor empty or null expression next (CEL returning a map {query: {...}} or null; in a conditional, write dyn(null) so both branches type-check: more ? {'query': {'from': n}} : dyn(null)) next returns null

The mapping receives all pages: responses (list) and response (the current page when evaluating per page). extract.items is evaluated per page and items are concatenated.

items.title: Discovery (fan-out)
items.text:
• A template with role: inventory produces inventory items: a key and a map of fields, cached in the state store with a TTL (default: 3x the job's effective interval).
  • A template or inline job with forEach runs once per inventory item of its parent (forEach.template or, for inline jobs, forEach.job), with parent.<field> available in forEach.vars CEL expressions.
  • Inventory jobs can also produce metrics (role: both).
  • Fan-out instances are scheduled with spread: the N child instances of a job are distributed over the interval rather than fired simultaneously. A newly discovered instance runs first within the jitter of its interval, so that the data of a discovery chain does not wait one interval per level.
  • Inventory changes (items added or removed) trigger a replan and the creation or removal of child instances. Series of removed instances become stale.
  • forEach.filter (CEL on parent) selects a subset of items (e.g. only networks with wireless product type).
  • The cardinality of fan-out is exposed (tapyr_job_instances) and capped by forEach.maxInstances (default 10000) to protect against runaway discovery.

items.title: Implementation notes
items.text:
• Job instances. A job runs as one instance per target (multi-target accounts) and per inventory item of its parent (fan-out). An instance is identified by the job name, the target and its variable values: devices[target=north-01,orgId=42]. The identity never appears in self-metric labels.
  • Variables. The variables of a child instance are those of its parent instance, overridden by its own forEach.vars, so a third level can use variables of the first (/orgs/{orgId}/networks/{networkId}/devices). Target params, then account params, fill the variables not set by discovery.
  • Implicit parents. A forEach.template that no job of the same account instantiates runs as an implicit job named <account>.<template>, with the template defaults and priority low.
  • Inventory. A successful run of an inventory job replaces the items of its instance (key and fields, cached in the state store). Items not refreshed within the TTL are dropped. Children are recomputed after every parent run, then created or removed; removed instances have their series retired.
  • Before the first parent run (or after a restart), children start from the cached inventory; without cache, they wait for the parent.
  • Spread. The instances of a fan-out get a phase derived from a hash of their instance key (the first 8 bytes of its SHA-256, so that keys differing only by their last characters still spread), uniformly distributed over the interval. The phase of an instance is stable across restarts and does not move when other instances come or go (an even spacing in key order would shift every phase on each inventory change).
  • First run of a new instance. An instance discovered while Tapyr runs (added by a run of its parent, not loaded from the cached inventory nor kept across a reload) runs first at a random point within the jitter of its interval (settings.collection.jitter, 10% by default), like a configured job at start. It then joins its phase, at the first slot at least half an interval after that first run: at most one more run per new instance, and the instances discovered together stay spread. The planner projects the steady state; every run goes through the budget engine, the first ones included.
  • Multi-target accounts. Target params override account params (base URL included), target secrets override account secrets, target labels are added between account and job labels, and CEL sees target.name, target.labels, target.params. Circuit breakers and perTarget sessions are per target.
  • Token auth. Token and login requests go through the budget engine with authRequest: true. Tokens are kept until expires_in (or expiresIn) minus refreshBefore (default 30s), persisted in the state store, encrypted with AES-GCM when TAPYR_STATE_KEY is set (a warning is logged once otherwise).
  • Token sessions. The jobs of an account share one token: per credential and token URL for oauth2_client_credentials, per account (or per target with perTarget) for session_login, whose login request uses the base URL of the target that opens the session. A changed auth configuration opens a new session. Renewals are serialized: concurrent requests wait for one token request. A token is renewed refreshBefore (30s for OAuth2) before it expires, or halfway through its lifetime when it is shorter; without expires_in or expiresIn, it lives 1 hour unless rejected. On authFailed, the token is dropped (from the store too) and the request retried once with a new one.
  • Order. A request obtains its credentials before its own budget reservation, so that a token request never waits behind a reservation held by the request it serves. Token requests are reserved as critical auth requests and count in maxConcurrentRequests. Their errors name the endpoint and the status, never the response body (it may carry tokens).

  • Stored tokens. A version byte, then the token (no TAPYR_STATE_KEY) or the nonce and AES-GCM ciphertext under SHA-256(TAPYR_STATE_KEY), authenticated with the session key. A token that cannot be opened (another key, or stored before a key was set) is ignored and replaced.

  • Logout. sessionLogin.logout (optional) declares a request (method, default POST, and path under the base URL) sent with the token applied, when the session replaces its token and when Tapyr stops. It goes through the budget engine as an auth request; its failures are logged at debug level and never fail a run. RutOS keeps sessions open after their token expires (its memory grows), hence this request.

  • Rejected credentials. A token or login request answered 400, 401 or 403 is a rejection: the session sends no other token or login request for 1 minute, then 2, 4... up to 1 hour, and the runs needing it fail at once with the rejection. A successful request, or a new session (changed secrets or auth configuration, after a reload), ends the backoff. A wrong password thus never hits the API, nor locks the account, at every run.
  • TLS. Account.spec.tls applies to every request of the account, auth requests included: caFile adds a PEM bundle to the system roots, insecureSkipVerify disables verification and logs a warning at every load. Accounts with TLS settings get their own HTTP transport; the others share one.
  • Plugins. A plugin is Go code registered in internal/auth/plugins (an explicit registry built by cmd/tapyr, no init side effects). It validates plugin.config at compile time, where {secret: <name>} values name account secrets, and creates an authenticator per account (or target) from: the base URL, the resolved secrets, a sender of auth requests through the budget engine, a sealed key-value store in the state store (encrypted with TAPYR_STATE_KEY like tokens), the clock, a logger and a read-only flag. Read-only (tapyr record, next to tapyr run), the store does not persist and the plugin must not renew credentials whose renewal invalidates the previous ones: it returns an error instead. It reports its token requests and its re-bootstrap condition, shown by tapyr_auth_reauth_required, /readyz (as a reason, without failing readiness) and the status API. A plugin also provides its simulator side (08-simulator.md).
  • aruba_central_classic. Verified against the Aruba developer documentation (access token management, OAuth, and the official pycentral SDK):
  • config: clientId, clientSecret, refreshToken (required) and accessToken (optional) as secret references, tokenPath (default /oauth2/token), refreshBefore (default 10m);
  • refresh: POST <baseURL>/oauth2/token?client_id=...&client_secret=...&grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=... (parameters in the query, as documented), answering access_token, refresh_token, token_type, expires_in (7200 seconds); the access token is applied as Authorization: Bearer;
  • every refresh returns a new refresh token, valid 15 days; the previous one is treated as spent. The new pair is written to the store before it is used. A crash between the answer and the write loses the pair: the refresh is the only request in flight for the account, and the README documents the re-bootstrap;
  • the stored pair records a hash of the bootstrap refresh token: a changed bootstrap secret (after a reload) replaces the stored pair, an unchanged one never does;
  • a refresh answered 400 or 401 sets the re-bootstrap condition: requests of the account fail without calling the API until the bootstrap secrets change; other failures are retried at the next request;
  • a request answered 401 triggers one refresh (serialized per account) and one retry.

items.title: Error classification
items.text: Condition Class Action Matches errors.rateLimited rate_limited Penalty via budget engine, retry after penalty if within run deadline Matches errors.authFailed auth OnAuthFailure, single retry if it returns true Matches errors.retryable, network error, timeout transient Retry with backoff Other 4xx client No retry, job run fails, logged with response excerpt (redacted) Response decoding error decode No retry, run fails Budget refusal budget No retry in this run, run marked skipped_budget

items.title: Retry policy
items.text:
• Exponential backoff with full jitter: sleep = random(0, min(maxBackoff, initialBackoff * multiplier^attempt)).
  • maxAttempts (default 4, including the first attempt).
  • Every retry goes through the budget engine as a retry (retry reserve).
  • A run has a deadline (default: its effective interval, capped at 10 minutes). Retries never extend a run beyond its deadline.
  • Only idempotent requests are retried (GET, HEAD, and POST explicitly marked idempotent).
  • Retried classes: transient (with backoff) and rate_limited (after the penalty set by the budget engine, which the next reservation waits for). auth is retried once when OnAuthFailure returns true (never for static auth types). client, decode and budget are not retried.
  • Every retry and every page of a run share the run deadline; a retry that cannot complete before it is not attempted.
  • Partial pagination failure: the run fails as a whole by default (no partial data emitted), unless extract.partial: true (then emitted samples are flagged with the self-metric tapyr_job_partial_runs_total).

items.title: Circuit breaker
items.text:
Per account (per target for multi-target accounts):

  • Opens after failureThreshold consecutive transient failures (default 5).
  • While open, requests are refused by the budget engine (circuit_open), so no quota is wasted.
  • After cooldown (default 2m, doubling up to 30m on repeated openings), half-open: one probe request (the next scheduled one). Success closes it; failure reopens it.
  • State exposed as tapyr_circuit_state{account, target} (0 closed, 1 half-open, 2 open).

items.title: Run outcome
items.text: Each run records: start, end, duration, requests (by class), pages, retries, items, samples produced, result (success, partial, failed, skipped_budget, skipped_overlap, skipped_circuit), error summary (redacted). Runs are kept in the state store (last 50 per job instance) and exposed in the status API.

items.title: Mapping language: CEL
items.text: Mappings use CEL (Common Expression Language, cel.dev/cel-go). Rationale in ADR 0002. Key properties: non Turing-complete (termination guaranteed), type-checked at compile time (errors surface in tapyr validate), cost-estimable, fast once compiled, extensible with custom functions.

items.title: CEL environment
items.text:
Variables available in extract expressions:

Variable Type Content response map Current page: status (int), headers (map of lowercase name to list of strings), body (dyn, decoded JSON: integral numbers that fit in int64 decode as int, other numbers as double, so IDs keep their precision and string(item.id) yields "123") responses list All pages (same shape), available in extract.post item dyn Current element of extract.items vars map(string, string) Request variables (discovery and params) parent map Parent inventory item fields (in forEach) account map name, labels, params (never secrets) target map name, labels, params (multi-target accounts) now timestamp Run start time (from the injected clock)

Variables are declared only where they are meaningful, so validate rejects, for example, item in extract.items:

Fields Variables extract.items, pagination stop, total, cursor, next response, vars, account, target, now extract.filter, metrics.*, info.*, inventory.* the above plus item extract.post.* responses, vars, account, target, now forEach.vars, forEach.filter parent, account, target, now request.query and request.body values { expr } vars, account, target, now sessionLogin.token, sessionLogin.expiresIn response, now

Custom functions:

Function Purpose default(value, fallback) Fallback when a field is absent or null toFloat(dyn) Number or numeric string to double, error otherwise parseTimestamp(string) / parseTimestamp(string, layout) RFC 3339 by default, or a Go layout fromUnix(number) / fromUnixMillis(number) Epoch to timestamp parseDuration(string) Human durations ("3d 4h", "01:02:03") to seconds parseBytes(string) Human sizes ("1.5 GB", "512 KiB") to bytes as a double (bytes() is a built-in CEL conversion and cannot be overloaded) lower(), upper() Unicode case conversion (item.name.lower()) trim, replace, split, ... cel-go string extension macToString(string) Normalize MAC address formats

The has() macro and optional types (?. syntax) are enabled to handle missing fields.

Compilation limits, configured in settings.mapping: max expression cost (maxCost, default 1000000), max items per run (maxItemsPerRun, default 100000), max samples per run (maxSamplesPerRun, default 200000).

A metric value expression may return int, uint, double or bool (true is 1); the result is converted to float64.

items.title: Extract block
items.text:
extract:
  items: "response.body.items"          # CEL -> list; default: response.body if it is a list
  filter: "item.status != 'unknown'"    # optional CEL -> bool
  metrics:
    - name: aruba_ap_clients
      type: gauge                       # gauge | counter
      help: Number of clients connected to the AP
      unit: ""                          # optional, Prometheus base units preferred
      value: "toFloat(item.client_count)"
      labels:
        serial: "item.serial"
        site: "default(item.site, '')"
      timestamp: "parseTimestamp(item.last_modified)"   # optional
      skipIf: "!has(item.client_count)"                 # optional CEL -> bool
  info:
    - name: aruba_ap_info
      labels:
        serial: "item.serial"
        model: "item.model"
        firmware: "item.firmware_version"
  inventory:                            # for role: inventory | both
    key: "item.serial"
    fields:
      serial: "item.serial"
      site: "item.site"
  post: []                              # optional metrics computed over all items
  • info metrics are gauges with value 1 and descriptive labels (standard _info pattern). Descriptive attributes belong there, not on every metric.
  • post entries can aggregate across items, e.g. value: "double(size(responses[0].body))" for a count.
  • Account labels, target labels and job labels are added to every sample. Conflicts: job > target > account > mapping (settings.mapping.labelConflict: error turns conflicts into run errors).
  • Empty-string label values are dropped (Prometheus semantics).
  • Label expressions return strings; ints, doubles and bools are converted to their string form, null gives an empty (dropped) label. Other types are mapping errors.
  • A mapping error on one item or one metric skips that sample and is counted (tapyr_mapping_errors_total); an error in extract.items fails the run.

items.title: Window values and counters
items.text:
Many APIs return values aggregated over a window ("bytes over the last 5 minutes") rather than cumulative counters.

  • Default: expose them as gauges named explicitly (meraki_uplink_sent_bytes_5m). This is honest and simple.
  • Optional reconstruction: type: counter with accumulate: true sums successive window values into a monotonic counter persisted in the state store. Requires non-overlapping windows (windowField or job interval aligned). Counter resets on restart are avoided by persistence; gaps are documented.
  • Native cumulative counters from APIs map directly to type: counter.

items.title: Internal metric model
items.text: Each sample: metric name, type, unit, help, label set (sorted), value (float64), timestamp (source timestamp or collection time), plus provenance (job instance, run id). Converted to each output format at the edge.

items.title: Series registry: staleness and deduplication
items.text:
Per job instance, the registry keeps the set of series emitted by the last successful run and the last timestamp sent per series and output.

  • Staleness: a series present in the previous successful run but absent from the current one is stale.
  • Prometheus pull: removed from the exposition.
  • Remote write: a stale marker sample (the Prometheus special NaN value 0x7ff0000000000002) is sent once.
  • OTLP: one data point with the FLAG_NO_RECORDED_VALUE flag is sent once.
  • When a job instance is removed (inventory change, config reload), all its series become stale.
  • A failed run does not cause staleness (series stay as-is until staleAfter, default 3x effective interval, after which they are removed from pull exposition and marked stale in push outputs).
  • Deduplication: when a sample carries a source timestamp lower than or equal to the last timestamp sent for that series and output, it is dropped (overlapping API windows). Counted in tapyr_samples_deduplicated_total.

items.title: Implementation notes
items.text:
• The registry is keyed by job instance. For an output with processing rules (see Processing), it also keeps the processed series last sent to that output, and staleness and deduplication use them; they are not persisted, but derived from the series of the snapshot with the current rules after a restart.
  • Pull exposition follows the registry directly: a successful run replaces the series of its instance; an instance whose last success is older than staleAfter is withdrawn; a removed instance is withdrawn at once.
  • Push outputs receive, per output, the samples that pass deduplication and the series to mark stale; the registry computes both.
  • Deduplication only concerns samples with a source timestamp; samples stamped with the collection time are never deduplicated.
  • The registry is snapshotted with the ledger (every 5 seconds and on shutdown): the series of every instance, and the last source timestamp sent per series and output.
  • The source timestamps of a series are forgotten when it goes stale, which bounds the registry to the live series. After a restart, instances of the snapshot that are no longer scheduled (removed from the configuration, or children waiting for the first run of their parent without a cached inventory) are withdrawn at the first check.

items.title: Processing
items.text:
An output may declare spec.processing, an ordered list of rules applied to the samples of the jobs sent to it only (ADR 0012), with the semantics of Prometheus metric_relabel_configs:

Action Fields Effect keep sourceLabels (required), separator (default ;), regex (default (.*)) keeps the samples whose joined source label values match drop same drops the samples whose joined source label values match labelkeep regex (required) keeps only the labels whose name matches labeldrop regex (required) removes the labels whose name matches
  • regex is RE2, fully anchored. __name__ is the metric name; a missing label is the empty string. Rules apply in order; a dropped sample stops at once.
  • Rules apply on the delivery of each output: after the mapping and the counter reconstruction, before deduplication and before the externalLabels of the output. Without rules, nothing changes.
  • Staleness follows the series the output receives: a series that a rule starts dropping (after a reload) or that labeldrop renames gets a stale marker once, at the next successful run of its instance. A rule change applies from that run.
  • Two samples of one run that end up with the same series and timestamp (a labeldrop removing the label that told them apart): the first is kept, the others are dropped and counted in tapyr_output_samples_dropped_total{reason="duplicate"}.
  • Samples removed by keep and drop are counted in tapyr_output_samples_filtered_total.
  • Self-metrics are never processed, on /metrics/self or pushed through an output.
  • tapyr validate rejects an unknown action, a missing or extra field, an invalid regex or label name, and a rule that would remove __name__ (labelkeep not matching it, labeldrop matching it); it warns about a keep or drop on __name__ alone that matches no metric of the jobs sent to the output.
  • Not yet: replace, labelmap, conditions in CEL, aggregation, an interval per output, sending on change (follow-ups of ADR 0012).

items.title: Timestamps
items.text:
• If timestamp is set in the mapping, the sample carries the source timestamp. Otherwise, the collection time (response received).
  • Push outputs always send timestamps.
  • Prometheus pull exposition omits timestamps by default (exposeTimestamps: false), as recommended by Prometheus; the latest value per series is exposed.
  • Out-of-order caveat: Prometheus remote write receivers may reject out-of-order samples unless out-of-order ingestion is enabled; VictoriaMetrics accepts them. See docs/outputs.md: the push engine splits a refused batch so that only the refused samples are lost, counted in tapyr_output_samples_dropped_total{reason="out_of_order"}.

items.title: Outputs
items.text:
All outputs implement:

type Output interface {
    Name() string
    Enqueue(batch model.Batch)           // non-blocking; drops with accounting when the queue is full
    Run(ctx context.Context) error       // sender loop
    Flush(ctx context.Context) error     // on shutdown
}

items.title: prometheus (pull)
items.text:
• Served by the main HTTP server on /metrics (collected data only; Tapyr's own metrics are on /metrics/self, see 07-self-observability.md).
  • Holds the samples of the last successful run of every job instance: a successful run replaces the series of its instance, a failed run keeps them (until staleAfter, see above). Content negotiation: Prometheus text format and OpenMetrics, gzip-compressed when the scraper accepts it (Accept-Encoding).
  • HELP and TYPE from the mapping. Metric name conflicts (same name, different type) are rejected at validation.

items.title: remote_write
items.text:
• Prometheus remote write 1.0 (protobuf + snappy), HTTP POST.
  • Batching (maxBatch, flushInterval), bounded queue (capacity, drop-oldest with accounting), retries with backoff on 5xx and 429 (respecting Retry-After), no retry on 4xx other than 429.
  • Metadata (HELP, TYPE) sent periodically.
  • Compatible targets: Prometheus (with the remote write receiver enabled), VictoriaMetrics (/api/v1/write), Grafana Mimir, Thanos Receive, Cortex.
  • Remote write 2.0 is not supported yet.

items.title: otlp
items.text:
• OTLP metrics over HTTP (protobuf) or gRPC.
  • Payloads are built directly with pmetric (go.opentelemetry.io/collector/pdata), not with the OpenTelemetry metrics SDK, which aggregates and cannot carry source timestamps (ADR 0008).
  • Mapping: gauge to OTLP Gauge; counter to OTLP Sum (monotonic, cumulative, start time = series first seen or persisted start). Labels to data point attributes. Resource attributes: service.name=tapyr, service.instance.id, tapyr.provider, tapyr.account (configurable), plus resourceAttributes.
  • Batching, bounded queue and retries as for remote write; honors OTLP partial success responses and throttling hints.

items.title: Implementation notes
items.text:
• Push engine (internal/output/push), shared by remote_write and otlp: the queue counts samples, stale markers included; when full, the oldest samples are dropped (queue_full). One request is in flight per output, so samples of a series leave in order. A batch is sent when it reaches maxBatch or when its oldest sample waited flushInterval. Network errors, 5xx and 429 are retried with exponential backoff (1s doubling up to 1m, full jitter), honoring Retry-After (capped at 5 minutes); a batch is retried until it succeeds or is pushed out by newer samples, so a slow backend costs memory up to capacity, never collection. Other 4xx drop the batch (rejected), except when the response mentions out of order, too old or out of bounds samples (out_of_order): such a backend refuses the whole request for one of its samples, so the batch is split in halves sent one after the other, a refused half is split further, and the samples refused alone are dropped (out_of_order). The spans of a split batch keep their order and stay the batch in flight; after 64 requests for one batch, the spans left are sent once each and dropped if refused. A retryable error during the split retries the current span with the backoff; a split batch can still be pushed out by newer samples during it. On shutdown, Flush sends what is queued within the shutdown deadline, without retry delays beyond it.
  • External labels are added to every sample; a label set by the sample wins.
  • Stale markers carry the time the series went stale (the run that no longer produced it, or the withdrawal). The output remembers the type and start time of the series it sent, so a marker is a gauge point when the series is unknown (after a restart).
  • Remote write sends Content-Encoding: snappy, Content-Type: application/x-protobuf, X-Prometheus-Remote-Write-Version: 0.1.0 and User-Agent: tapyr/<version>; the time series of a request are sorted by labels with their samples in time order. Metadata (TYPE, HELP, unit) of every metric family seen is sent in a request of its own on the first send and every 1 minute.
  • OTLP groups samples by resource (provider and account of the job instance) and metric name; the instrumentation scope is github.com/kentrow/tapyr with the Tapyr version. service.instance.id is a random identifier created on first start and kept in the state store (resourceAttributes may override it). HTTP: POST to the endpoint, with /v1/metrics appended when the endpoint has no path; gRPC: http:// endpoints are plaintext, https:// use TLS with the system roots. Retryable: HTTP 429, 502, 503, 504 and gRPC UNAVAILABLE, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED (with RetryInfo); rejected data points of a partial success are counted as rejected. The start time of a cumulative sum is the first time the output saw the series in this process, or its earliest timestamp when a source timestamp is older; a restart starts the sums again, which receivers treat as a reset.
  • Counter reconstruction (accumulate: true): per job instance and series, the store keeps the running total and the last window counted (the windowField value, else the sample timestamp). A sample whose window was already counted adds nothing; negative window values are mapping errors. The totals are persisted with the ledger (table accumulators) and dropped when the series goes stale or its instance is removed, a counter reset receivers handle.

items.title: Multiple outputs
items.text: A job sends to all outputs by default, or to the subset listed in spec.outputs. Each output has its own queue: a slow backend never blocks collection or other outputs, and its own processing rules: a local backend can stay complete next to a reduced hosted one.

items.title: 07 - Self-observability ("monitoring of monitoring")
items.text: Tapyr must answer, at any time: are my API calls healthy, how much quota is left, when will it run out, are my jobs fresh, are my outputs keeping up?

items.title: Endpoints
items.text:
Path Content /metrics Collected data (when a prometheus output is configured) /metrics/self Tapyr's own metrics (always available) /healthz Liveness: process alive, main loops running. 200 or 503 /readyz Readiness: config loaded, state store open, outputs initialized. 200 or 503 with JSON reasons

Self-metrics can also be pushed: setting selfMetrics.outputs: [name] in Settings sends them through the given outputs (with job="tapyr_self" semantics), so Tapyr can be monitored even where nothing scrapes it.

items.title: Label conventions
items.text:
• provider, account, target (empty when not multi-target), job (job name, not instance), endpoint (templated path), limit (limit name), scope_kind (dimension names joined, e.g. account,var:organizationId), output.
  • Never concrete IDs, serials, IPs or resolved URLs in self-metric labels. Per-scope-key detail (e.g. per organization) is available in the status API, not in metrics, except for quota scopes whose cardinality is bounded by configuration (account, target, credential): those expose a scope label with a non-sensitive key (account=acme-meraki).

items.title: HTTP calls
items.text: Metric Type Labels Notes tapyr_http_requests_total counter provider, account, job, endpoint, code, class tapyr_http_request_duration_seconds histogram provider, account, endpoint tapyr_http_response_size_bytes histogram provider, endpoint tapyr_http_retries_total counter provider, account, job, reason tapyr_http_in_flight gauge provider, account

items.title: Budget
items.text: Metric Type Labels Notes tapyr_budget_limit gauge provider, limit, scope effective max for the window (after learning and share) tapyr_budget_used gauge provider, limit, scope consumed in the current window tapyr_budget_remaining gauge provider, limit, scope internal estimate tapyr_budget_remaining_observed gauge provider, limit, scope from headers, when available tapyr_budget_external_usage gauge provider, limit, scope estimated consumption by other clients in the window tapyr_budget_reserve_remaining gauge provider, limit, scope retry reserve left tapyr_budget_window_end_timestamp_seconds gauge provider, limit, scope tapyr_budget_exhaustion_eta_seconds gauge provider, limit, scope absent when no exhaustion is projected tapyr_budget_wait_seconds histogram provider, limit time spent waiting for rate or concurrency tapyr_budget_refusals_total counter provider, account, job, reason quota_exhausted, penalized, circuit_open, deadline tapyr_budget_rate_limited_total counter provider, account, limit 429 received tapyr_budget_unexpected_429_total counter provider, account 429 not predicted by any internal limit tapyr_budget_limit_mismatch gauge provider, limit 1 when headers disagree with the declared max tapyr_plan_feasible gauge provider, limit, scope 1 feasible, 0 infeasible tapyr_plan_recomputations_total counter reason start, reload, interval, limit_learned, inventory, projection (04-budget-engine.md, Replan on projection)

items.title: Jobs
items.text: Metric Type Labels Notes tapyr_job_runs_total counter provider, account, job, result tapyr_job_run_duration_seconds histogram provider, job tapyr_job_last_success_timestamp_seconds gauge provider, account, job min across instances tapyr_job_desired_interval_seconds gauge provider, account, job tapyr_job_effective_interval_seconds gauge provider, account, job tapyr_job_lag_seconds gauge provider, account, job max delay vs schedule across instances tapyr_job_instances gauge provider, account, job fan-out size tapyr_job_series gauge provider, account, job series produced by the last runs tapyr_job_pages_per_run histogram provider, job tapyr_job_partial_runs_total counter provider, account, job tapyr_mapping_errors_total counter provider, job, metric tapyr_samples_deduplicated_total counter provider, job

items.title: Auth and resilience
items.text: Metric Type Labels Notes tapyr_auth_token_requests_total counter provider, account, result tapyr_auth_token_expiry_timestamp_seconds gauge provider, account tapyr_auth_reauth_required gauge provider, account 1 when manual re-bootstrap is needed tapyr_circuit_state gauge provider, account, target 0 closed, 1 half-open, 2 open

items.title: Outputs
items.text: Metric Type Labels Notes tapyr_output_samples_sent_total counter output tapyr_output_samples_dropped_total counter output, reason queue_full, rejected, out_of_order, duplicate (samples that processing rules made identical) tapyr_output_samples_filtered_total counter output removed by the keep and drop processing rules of the output (intended, not a loss) tapyr_output_send_failures_total counter output, class tapyr_output_queue_samples gauge output tapyr_output_send_duration_seconds histogram output tapyr_output_last_success_timestamp_seconds gauge output

items.title: Process and config
items.text:
Metric Type Labels Notes tapyr_build_info gauge version, revision, goversion tapyr_config_last_reload_success gauge tapyr_config_last_reload_timestamp_seconds gauge tapyr_state_flush_duration_seconds histogram tapyr_state_flush_failures_total counter

Plus standard Go and process collectors.

items.title: Logs
items.text:
• log/slog, JSON by default (text for local development).
  • Standard fields: ts (from the injected clock), level, msg, component, and when relevant provider, account, target, job, instance, run_id, endpoint, status, duration_ms, reason.
  • Per-request logs at debug level only. info logs: lifecycle, config reloads, plan changes, circuit transitions, quota exhaustion, auth events.
  • Repetitive warnings are rate-limited (same message and key at most once per minute, with a suppressed count).
  • Redaction: headers Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie, X-*-Key, X-*-Token and any configured secret value are replaced by [REDACTED]. A test asserts that no configured secret value appears in any log line produced by the test suite.

items.title: Implementation notes
items.text:
• Registry. client_golang with a registry owned by tapyr run, never the global one. Counters and histograms belong to the process and survive reloads; gauges describing the running configuration (budgets, jobs, circuits, tokens, outputs) are computed at scrape time from the current generation, so a reload never leaves gauges of removed jobs behind.
  • Hooks. The budget engine, the executor, the token manager and the outputs report events through small observer interfaces of their own packages; internal/selfobs implements them. Packages never import client_golang except internal/selfobs.
  • Budget scopes. Quota gauges carry a scope label only for scopes whose dimensions are bounded by configuration (instance, provider, account, target, credential, endpoint; the credential appears as its keyed hash). For scopes partitioned by a variable, one series per limit carries the most constrained key (lowest remaining fraction) with scope set to the dimension names (var:organizationId), never the value; every key is in the status API.
  • Projection. tapyr_budget_exhaustion_eta_seconds extrapolates the consumption rate since the start of a fixed window and is exposed only when the remaining budget runs out before the window ends. Rolling windows never end: at a steady rate their consumption stays level, so no exhaustion is projected for them.
  • Waits. tapyr_budget_wait_seconds observes the time a granted reservation waited, labelled with the limit that held it last (none for penalties and priority waits).
  • Durations are measured on the injected clock; histograms use the default buckets for seconds, powers of 4 from 256 bytes to 64 MiB for sizes and powers of 2 up to 1024 for pages.
  • Push. selfMetrics.outputs gathers the registry every selfMetrics.interval (default 30s) and enqueues the result in the given outputs as the pseudo job instance tapyr_self (histograms as _bucket, _sum and _count counters). Self-metrics keep their own job label; no label is added. They bypass the series registry: no deduplication and no stale markers.
  • Health. /healthz answers 503 when the flush loop (every 5 seconds) has not ticked for 30 seconds on the injected clock. /readyz answers 503 with {"ready": false, "reasons": [...]} until the state store answers a ping, the configuration is loaded and every output has started its sender loop. conditions lists the accounts whose credentials need a manual re-bootstrap (auth plugins), without failing the readiness: the other accounts keep collecting.
  • Redaction. A slog handler wraps every logger of tapyr run: values of configured secrets and of tokens obtained by authenticators (4 characters or more; a shorter secret is reported at startup as too short to be redacted) are replaced by [REDACTED] in messages and string attributes, and attributes named after a redacted header are replaced whole. The CLI test helpers fail any test whose captured logs contain a secret of its environment.

items.title: Shipped dashboards and alerts
items.text:
• dashboards/tapyr-overview.json: providers health, budgets (used vs limit, projections, external usage), job freshness, errors, outputs.

  • docs/alerts.md (and an example rules file in examples/): quota exhaustion projected before window end, unexpected 429s, job stale for 3x interval, circuit open, re-auth required, output dropping samples, plan infeasible.

  • dashboards/tapyr-overview.json has rows Health (plan, failed runs, unexpected 429, open circuits, re-bootstrap conditions, version), Quotas (left, projected exhaustion, consumption against the limit with external usage), Jobs (runs by result, lag, desired and effective intervals), Provider calls (requests by status, retries, p95 durations and waits) and Outputs, with datasource and provider variables.

  • The rules are in examples/alerts/tapyr-alerts.yaml (14 alerts, severity critical, warning or info), with promtool unit tests (make alerts-check). A Go test checks that every metric used by the dashboard and the rules is documented in the tables above, and that every alert has its section in docs/alerts.md.
  • The self-metrics carry the job label of the Tapyr job: a scrape of /metrics/self needs honor_labels: true, or the label becomes exported_job.

items.title: Why
items.text: Two of the built-in providers cannot be fully tested against real platforms by the maintainer: Aruba Central not at all, Meraki only through a DevNet sandbox organization with a few devices. More generally, contributors and users need to develop, test and demo providers without vendor access, and nobody can safely test quota exhaustion against a production API. The simulator makes every provider testable, and its rate-limit enforcement makes the budget engine testable end-to-end.

items.title: Principles
items.text:
• Same definition, two consumers. The simulator reads the provider package: the Provider document (limits, pagination, auth, error semantics) and the package's sim/ directory (routes, fixtures, scenarios). Limits are declared once.
  • Package-internal kinds. Simulation and Scenario documents live only in a package's sim/ directory; user configuration paths reject them.
  • Server-side enforcement reuses the budget package (rate, concurrency, quota windows) in "enforcer" mode, so the simulator returns 429, Retry-After and quota headers exactly as declared.
  • Deterministic by default (seeded randomness), reproducible in CI.
  • Runs on the injected clock. Automated tests share a fake clock between Tapyr and the simulator and run 24 simulated hours in seconds; --time-scale accelerates the real clock for demos and manual tests.

items.title: sim/sim.yaml
items.text:
apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
kind: Simulation
metadata:
  name: meraki-dashboard
spec:
  inventory:                          # synthetic inventory generator (generic sets)
    seed: 42
    sets:
      - { name: organizations, count: 2 }
      - { name: networks, parent: organizations, count: 5 }   # count items per parent item
      - { name: devices, parent: networks, count: 20 }        # per network
  auth:
    accept:                           # credentials the simulator accepts
      bearer: ["sim-api-key"]
  headers:                            # quota headers emitted, mapped to limit names
    X-RateLimit-Limit-day: "limit:daily.max"
    X-RateLimit-Remaining-day: "limit:daily.remaining"
  routes:
    - method: GET
      path: /organizations
      response:
        template: fixtures/organizations.json.tmpl
    - method: GET
      path: /organizations/{organizationId}/devices/availabilities
      pagination: link_header         # simulator paginates the generated list
      response:
        # values evolving over simulated time come from template helpers,
        # e.g. {{ flap $d "status" "10m" "online:0.95" "offline:0.03" "alerting:0.02" }}
        template: fixtures/availabilities.json.tmpl
  • basePath (default /) is the path prefix of the API (the path part of the provider base URL); routes are relative to it.
  • Credentials are checked the way the Provider declares its auth (bearer: Authorization: Bearer <one of accept.bearer>; header: the declared header with one of accept.header, formatted with the format of the auth; basic: one of accept.basic). Wrong or missing credentials get the provider's authFailed status.
  • A route with pagination serves the items of its fixture (a JSON array) page by page. The pagination parameters are not redeclared: they come from the job templates requesting that path, or from the provider default.
  • Fixtures are JSON templates (Go text/template with helpers: range over inventory, deterministic pseudo-random values, counters increasing with time, timestamps from the simulated clock).
  • Static JSON fixtures (e.g. recorded) are supported directly.
  • Unknown routes return 404 like a real API.

items.title: Synthetic inventory and templated fixtures
items.text:
The inventory is generic: the core knows sets of items and parents, never vendor objects, and dynamics are template helpers rather than per-route declarations.

  • Every generated item has name (its set), index (position in its set, from 0), n (position under its parent, from 0), key (<set>-<index>) and parent (the parent item, or nil). Sets are generated in declaration order; a parent set must come first. The inventory is fixed for the lifetime of the simulator.
  • response.template (instead of response.file) is a Go text/template rendering JSON. Its data: .vars (route variables), .inventory (items by set name), .now (simulated time) and .query (query parameters). Helpers, all deterministic for a given seed:
  • items "set" and children "set" item (items of a set, or those under an item), find "set" "key" (the item with that key), where list "field" value;
  • id item "prefix" (a stable identifier), serial item "XXXX-XXXX-XXXX" (X letters, 9 digits), mac item, ipv4 item (in 10.0.0.0/8), pick item "field" "a" "b" ... (one value per item and field), num item "field" lo hi (an integer in [lo, hi], fixed per item and field);
  • dynamics: rand item "field" min max (a float in [min, max] rounded to 3 decimals, fixed per item; use num for integers such as counts and identifiers), walk item "field" min max "10m" (a float, like rand, that moves inside [min, max] every period), flap item "field" "10m" "online:0.95" "offline:0.03" "alerting:0.02" (a weighted state, drawn again every period), counter item "field" ratePerSecond (grows with simulated time, for native counters);
  • json value (JSON encoding), ts "2006-01-02T15:04:05Z07:00" time, unix time, ago "5m" (now minus a duration), add, sub, mul, div, mod, seq n, last list.
  • Dynamics depend only on the seed, the item, the field and the period number, so a contract test at a fixed simulated time always sees the same values.
  • Static fixtures (file) keep working, recorded ones included. A fixture path may use the route variables (file: devices/{id}.json): a missing file answers 404, like an unknown object. A fixture that does not render or parse answers 500 with its cause, which the contract test of tapyr provider lint shows.
  • The simulator loads its package at startup: restart it after editing a fixture. Limitations to keep in mind when imitating an API: quota reset headers (limit:<name>.reset) are sent as a number of seconds until the reset, and the status of a route is fixed (errors come from scenarios, not from the fixtures).
  • spec.portOffset places the simulator in tapyr sim --all: it listens at --listen-base plus this offset, so that adding a package moves no other simulator. Packages without one take the offsets after the largest declared one, in provider name order; two packages declaring the same offset are an error. The built-in packages declare 0 (aruba-central-classic) to 4 (teltonika-rutos).
  • response.itemsField (a dotted path, for example data or aps) paginates the list found at that path of the document instead of a top-level array: the simulator replaces the list by the requested page and keeps the rest of the envelope (counts and totals are computed by the template over the whole list).

items.title: Scenarios
items.text:
sim/scenarios/*.yaml, selected with --scenario. A scenario overlays faults on top of the default behavior, on a timeline:

apiVersion: tapyr/v1alpha1
kind: Scenario
metadata:
  name: bad-day
spec:
  steps:
    - at: 0s
      externalConsumption: { limit: daily, ratePerHour: 300 }   # another tool eats the quota
    - at: 2h
      latency: { p50: 800ms, p99: 5s }
    - at: 3h
      errors: { routes: ["/organizations/**"], status: 503, ratio: 0.3 }  # globs as in appliesTo.endpoints
      for: 20m
    - at: 6h
      outage: true                                               # connections dropped
      for: 10m
    - at: 8h
      tokenExpiry: true                                          # invalidate tokens, force 401

Built-in scenarios for every provider: default, quota-tight (undersized daily quota), bad-day.

A step applies from at until at + for, or until the end when for is omitted. at is measured from the simulator start, in simulated time. Step actions:

  • limits overrides the max of named quota limits, for example limits: { daily: { max: 1500 } }.
  • externalConsumption makes another client consume a quota at a steady hourly rate, spread over time: each window receives what was consumed during it, however long ago the previous request came (a minute window gets at most a minute of it).
  • errors gives a status to a ratio of the requests to matching routes.
  • fixtures replaces the fixture of routes during the step (fixtures: { "/orgs/{orgId}/networks": "fixtures/networks-after.json" }), to simulate inventory changes.
  • latency: { p50: 800ms, p99: 5s } delays responses following a log-normal distribution with these quantiles (seeded), in simulated time. The delay is the processing time of the server: a request is counted by the limits when it arrives, then answered after the delay, holding its concurrency slot; a refusal (429) answers at once. Counted after the delay, requests sent at the pace of a rate limit would reach it bunched together and get 429 the client could not foresee.
  • outage: true closes connections without a response (the client sees a network error) while the step is active; a step without for lasts until the end.
  • tokenExpiry: true invalidates, when the step starts, every token issued before it (the next request gets authFailed).

items.title: Auth and pagination
items.text:
With oauth2_client_credentials, the simulator serves the path of the provider's token URL (rendered without account params, so its defaults point to the simulator) and accepts the client credentials listed in auth.accept.clients (clientId, clientSecret, in the Authorization header or the form); with session_login, it serves the login path under basePath and accepts a JSON body carrying both values of one of the auth.accept.logins username and password pairs. Both issue opaque tokens valid for auth.tokenLifetime (default 10m, simulated time), then accepted as the provider applies them (bearer, header with format, or cookie); expired tokens get the authFailed status. The token endpoint answers access_token, token_type and expires_in; the login endpoint answers {"token": ..., "expiresIn": <seconds>}, or the auth.loginResponse fixture with {token} and {expiresIn} replaced, to match the shape the provider's token expression reads. Token and login requests are checked against the limits as auth requests.

A provider whose auth is a plugin is simulated by the plugin itself: the plugin registers a simulator side that serves its token endpoints and validates its tokens, with the credentials of auth.accept.plugin (free-form, read by the plugin).

Pagination page and cursor are served like offset and link_header (expression is client-side only); with cursor, the next cursor is an opaque value in the X-Next-Cursor response header (absent on the last page), read by templates with default(response.headers['x-next-cursor'][0], '').

items.title: CLI
items.text:
tapyr sim --provider meraki-dashboard [--provider-path ./providers] [--scenario bad-day] [--listen :8081] [--time-scale 60] [--seed 42]
tapyr sim --all --listen-base 127.0.0.1:8081   # one simulator per provider, at --listen-base plus its portOffset

--time-scale N runs the simulated clock N times faster than real time (windows, refills, penalties and scenario steps follow it). It is meant for demos and manual tests; automated tests share a fake clock between Tapyr and the simulator instead.

The simulator exposes one endpoint of its own, GET /_sim/status: a JSON object with the provider and its package version, the served routes, the number of requests received, the simulated time, the active scenario, stats (requests served, rate limited by reason, injected errors, tokens issued, dropped connections, sessions, requests per route) and the state of the quotas. Useful to cross-check Tapyr's self-metrics in demos.

items.title: Record mode
items.text:
tapyr record captures real API responses, anonymized, to build fixtures for a provider package or to attach responses to a bug report. It writes outside the repository: nothing enters it before a review.

tapyr record --config ./config --job rms-devices [--job ...] --out ./recordings/rms [--anonymize ./anonymize.yaml]
  • Every instance of the selected jobs runs once, through the budget engine. Children of fan-outs run once their parent has run.
  • It opens the state store of the configuration read-only (with TAPYR_STATE_KEY), so that it can run next to tapyr run: the store is never written, auth plugins read their stored state and do not renew credentials whose renewal invalidates the previous ones (a rotating refresh token, which tapyr run would then hold spent). Such a plugin uses the stored access token until its expiry, then fails with a message instead of renewing it. Other tokens (OAuth2 client credentials, session logins) are obtained in memory and not taken from the store: their sessions belong to tapyr run, and a logout would end them.
  • --out receives one JSON file per page (<job>/<n>.json, anonymized), index.yaml (method, templated path, pseudonymized variables, status, rate-limit headers, file per page) and report.txt. Request credentials and response headers other than the rate-limit headers of the provider (sync headers and Retry-After) are never written.
  • Default rules replace, by key name and by value pattern: serial numbers, MAC addresses, IMEI, IMSI, ICCID, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, hostnames, emails, phone numbers, names (keys name, site or ending in _name/Name), identifiers (keys id or ending in _id/Id, with the same pseudonym in path variables, so that fixtures stay consistent), coordinates and addresses (keys containing address, and street, city, zip, zipcode, postcode, postal_code). Pseudonyms keep the format: MACs become locally administered, IPv4 addresses move to 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24, IPv6 to 2001:db8::/32, emails to example.com, serials and identifiers keep their length and character classes (every letter and digit becomes an ASCII one, so no character of the value is kept), numbers stay numbers. They come from an HMAC with a random per-recording key that is never written.
  • --anonymize adds rules (replace: [{path: "data[*].company_name", as: name}]) and exceptions (keep: ["data[*].model"]); paths are dotted, with [*] for every element.
  • report.txt lists every replaced path with its rule and count, never an original value, for review before anything is committed. The recording is meant to be turned into static fixtures by hand (file routes).

items.title: Contract tests
items.text:
Each provider package's tests/ directory holds the expected samples of its templates run against the simulator with a fixed seed. tapyr provider lint and the CI run them: a change in mapping or fixtures that changes the produced series must update the expected file explicitly.

  • tests/contract.yaml holds the Account and Job documents run by the test; $SIM_URL is replaced by the URL of the simulator with its base path, and $SIM_ADDR by the URL without it (for base URLs that add the path themselves), before the documents are parsed; secrets are read from tests/contract.env (KEY=VALUE lines of simulator credentials), never from the environment, and the account uses the credentials accepted by the simulator.
  • tapyr provider lint <dir> validates the package, compiles its templates, lints its dashboards and runs the contract test: the simulator and the collector share a fake clock starting at 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z with seed 42; every job instance runs once (children after their parents), and the samples are compared with tests/expected.prom (Prometheus exposition, sorted, without timestamps). --update writes the file instead.
